entry.title: SAP-RPT-1.5 Is Now Generally Available: More Accurate Predictions, Better Explainability, What’s New
entry.content:
SAP-RPT-1.5 Is Now Generally Available: More Accurate Predictions, Better Explainability, and What’s Next

Predictive AI is becoming an increasingly important part of enterprise decision-making. Over the past few months, teams have been putting SAP-RPT models to work across real-world scenarios—from demand forecasting and high-volume classification to discovering patterns hidden within complex relational data.

These experiences raised an important question: How can we make predictions even more accurate while also making them easier for business users to understand and trust?

That question helped shape the next evolution of the SAP-RPT family.

We are excited to announce the general availability of SAP-RPT-1.5, bringing improved prediction accuracy, particularly for complex and high-cardinality scenarios, together with a new approach to explainability that makes predictions more intuitive for business users.

In this post, we’ll look at where SAP-RPT-1 is already creating value, what’s new in SAP-RPT-1.5, the available model variants, and what’s coming next.

Where SAP-RPT-1 Is Making an Impact

SAP-RPT-1 has already been applied to a growing range of enterprise use cases across finance, supply chain, sustainability, retail, and governance, risk, and compliance.

Combining Document AI with Predictive Intelligence

One of the most interesting applications has been the combination of Document AI and SAP-RPT-1 for high-volume, rule-intensive classification.

A great example is automated tax code determination with Clariant.

Clariant processes thousands of vendor invoices every year. These invoices are often unstructured PDFs and can be written in the local language of the supplier. Determining the correct VAT code requires consideration of several factors, including jurisdiction, supplier type, material, and place of supply.

Using Document AI to extract the relevant information and SAP-RPT-1 to predict the appropriate VAT code, the team built a working MVP in just four days and achieved 90% prediction accuracy during the pilot.

Looking ahead, the goal is to automate up to 32,000 invoices per year, with an automation rate of up to 98%, while expanding quality coverage from approximately 4% spot-check sampling to 100% of processed invoices.

Supporting Agentic Sales Order Creation

The same combination is also being explored for agentic sales order creation.

Instead of manually creating sales orders in SAP S/4HANA based on unstructured emails and documents, an AI agent can use Document AI to extract the available information and SAP-RPT-1 to predict additional fields required to complete the order.

This enables a more automated process while still leveraging the structured business context available in enterprise data.

Expanding Across Enterprise Scenarios

SAP-RPT-1 is also being applied to a broader set of business challenges:

  • Payment matching: Up to 90% match accuracy without requiring historical model training.
  • Working capital management: Up to 54% reduction in mean invoice approval date prediction error compared with a heavily tuned narrow AI model.
  • Sustainability: Automated account and cost object determination for tens of thousands of uploaded carbon-data entries, saving several working days.
  • Supply chain and logistics: Prediction of delivery delays and logistics destinations.
  • Finance and procurement: Classification and prediction tasks such as payment delays and material groups.

These examples demonstrate that SAP-RPT-1 is not limited to a single business process. It is designed as a general-purpose prediction engine for relational enterprise data.

What’s New in SAP-RPT-1.5?

SAP-RPT-1.5 introduces improvements across three key areas:

Prediction accuracy, throughput, and explainability.

More Accurate Predictions for Complex, High-Cardinality Data

SAP-RPT-1.5 delivers stronger prediction performance across a wide range of classification scenarios.

On SAP’s benchmark suite covering 166 real-world classification tasks, SAP-RPT-1.5 demonstrates strong performance overall, with particularly notable improvements on high-cardinality classification problems.

This is especially relevant for enterprise tabular AI, where datasets often contain many unique values and complex relationships.

SAP also evaluated SAP-RPT-1.5 on publicly available benchmarks. On the SALT enterprise tabular benchmark, SAP-RPT-1.5 demonstrated leading performance compared with other tabular foundation models as well as per-task tuned models.

For teams using the API, the maximum number of query rows per API call has also increased from 128 to 512, making larger prediction batches easier to handle.

You can find additional benchmarking details in the SAP-RPT-1.5 model card.

Why Accuracy Improvements Matter

In enterprise scenarios, even a few percentage points of additional accuracy can have a meaningful business impact.

Better predictions can mean:

  • Fewer manual corrections
  • Earlier identification of risks
  • Higher automation rates
  • Faster processing of business transactions
  • More consistent decision-making
  • Reduced operational effort

Whether the use case is tax code determination, material classification, payment delay prediction, logistics assignment, or supplier delivery prediction, improved accuracy can translate directly into better business outcomes.

Explainability: Explain by Example

One of the most exciting additions in SAP-RPT-1.5 is a new approach to explainability.

Traditional feature importance can tell you which columns influenced a prediction. SAP-RPT-1.5 goes a step further by showing which historical rows most influenced the prediction.

In other words, the model can explain a prediction by example.

Imagine a sales order scenario. Instead of simply saying that material group was the most influential feature, SAP-RPT-1.5 can also identify previous sales orders that closely resemble the current transaction.

For business users, this provides a much more tangible explanation:

“This prediction is similar to these previous business cases.”

This example-based explanation is particularly useful for users who naturally reason through comparisons with past business decisions.

It can also help teams build greater confidence in AI-driven recommendations by giving stakeholders a concrete reference for why a prediction makes sense.

SAP-RPT-1.5 Model Variants

SAP-RPT-1.5 is now generally available through SAP’s generative AI hub and is priced at the same level as RPT-1.

Two variants are available:

SAP-RPT-1.5

This is the default option and was previously known as the -small model.

It provides strong performance across a broad range of use cases and is the recommended starting point for most scenarios.

SAP-RPT-1.5-large

This variant is designed for more demanding scenarios, particularly:

  • Datasets with more than 100 columns
  • Use cases where maximizing prediction accuracy is the primary objective
  • More complex tabular prediction scenarios

More information is available in the SAP Help Portal.

What’s Coming Next: Tabular Orchestration

One of the most common questions from customers is:

How do we efficiently work with millions of historical records?

SAP-RPT models operate within a fixed context window. When a dataset contains millions of rows, selecting the most relevant historical records to provide as context becomes an important part of the prediction workflow.

Today, teams often need to manage this process themselves.

To simplify this, SAP is introducing tabular orchestration as a managed workflow on SAP’s generative AI hub, targeted for general availability in August 2026.

The concept is simple:

  1. Register your data table.
  2. Configure the prediction scenario at design time.
  3. Submit prediction requests at runtime.
  4. The workflow automatically retrieves and selects the most relevant context rows.

Tabular orchestration will also provide centralized management for model configuration and invocation, with context registration, model routing, and lifecycle management built into the workflow.

As the SAP-RPT family evolves and additional tabular foundation models become available, this orchestration layer is intended to provide a governed and repeatable foundation for enterprise predictive AI.

More details are expected closer to the September 2026 release.

Getting Started with SAP-RPT-1.5

SAP-RPT-1.5 is now available in the model library of SAP’s generative AI hub.

If you are new to the RPT model family, the RPT Playground is a simple way to explore the capabilities of the model using your own data or SAP-provided use-case samples, without requiring an initial setup.

You can explore the RPT Playground to get started.

For those ready to integrate SAP-RPT into predictive and tabular AI scenarios, our step-by-step guide walks through the process from model deployment to your first inference.

The SAP-RPT-1.5 model card is also a valuable resource for understanding capabilities, limitations, benchmarking results, and best practices for responsible adoption and governance.

Final Thoughts

SAP-RPT-1.5 represents another step toward making predictive AI more accurate, scalable, and understandable for enterprise use cases.

With stronger performance on complex and high-cardinality data, larger API batches, and the new “explain by example” capability, teams can not only generate better predictions but also provide business users with more intuitive reasons behind those predictions.

And with tabular orchestration on the horizon, the focus is shifting from simply building individual predictions to creating governed, reusable, and scalable predictive AI capabilities across the enterprise.

We’re excited to see how you use SAP-RPT-1.5 in your own scenarios.

What predictive use cases are you exploring with SAP-RPT? Share your experiences and ideas in the comments.

entry.title: SAP RPT 1.5: Where Explainability Makes Responsible AI Real
entry.content:
Note: This blog discusses explainability in SAP RPT 1.5, the enterprise Relational Pretrained Transformer for tabular and relational data, and the successor to SAP-RPT-1. The security foundations of the previous release are covered SAP-RPT-1: A Revolutionary Tabular ML Model and OWASP ML Top 10 Compliance. This post shows why explainability must be built into inference, and how RPT 1.5 returns an explanation with every prediction.

The Challenge: A Right Answer Isn't Enough Without the "Why"

Trust in a model rests on a simple expectation: the reasoning behind its output should be open to inspection. It is not enough for a model to be right; there must be a way to establish why it was right, and to confirm it was not right for the wrong reasons.

That "why" is Explainability, and it is firmly rooted in SAP's approach to Responsible and Ethical AI (see the SAP Global AI Ethics Policy and the SAP AI Ethics Handbook for more information).

Take a conventional classification or regression model, the kind trained on historical data and widely available in open-source libraries. Such a model returns a prediction and little else: it carries no indication of which inputs shaped that prediction or how much each one mattered. A strong accuracy score does not fill this gap. Accuracy measures only how often the model agrees with historical outcomes; it says nothing about which features the model actually relied on to get there. And when a model decides who is promoted, who receives a loan, or who is flagged for review, the features it relied on are the entire concern, precisely the thing these models leave unsaid.

(This is a deliberate contrast with SAP RPT 1.5, discussed later. RPT 1.5 uses in-context learning: it does not predict from patterns baked into training data, but from the input data provided with each request.)

A small, concrete example makes this easy to see.

When a Conventional Model Can't Explain Itself

For this example, the model is a conventional open-source classification model, trained on historical data and returning only an answer with no explanation of how it was reached.

Consider a promotion dataset: nine labelled employees, four features (Name, Age, Gender, Performance_Rating), and a target column, Promotion (Yes/No). Please note that this example is only for demonstration purposes. Model predictions alone should never account for promotion decisions, and in case AI is to assist promotion decisions, the same should undergo AI Ethics Assessment and be implemented with  appropriate safeguards. Once trained, the model is asked to predict the Promotion outcome for a new, unlabelled record, Zoey:

#

Name

Age

Performance_Rating

Promotion

Zoey

To Predict


This is a classification problem on structured, tabular data, not a task for a Large Language Model.

The conventional model predicts Yes with a confidence of 0.75. On the surface, nothing looks wrong: the performance rating is solid, the prediction is confident, and the decision would pass review without a second glance.

Now change a single value, and not one in Zoey's input record. A different employee's name is edited in the training data: Ivanka (Row 9) becomes Zelda. Zoey's own record, including age, gender, and performance rating, is left untouched, and every other value across both tables is identical.

Change applied to training data

Predicted outcome for Zoey

Row 9 named Ivanka

Yes

Row 9 renamed to Zelda (name only, all else identical)

No


Zoey's prediction flips from Yes to No, and the only thing that changed was someone else's name in the training data. Nothing about Zoey moved; the age, gender, and performance rating that should determine the outcome are exactly as before.

This is not a rounding error. It means the model is deciding promotions partly on the basis of names, an attribute that has no bearing on the decision at all. Worse, the influence leaks across records: one person's name reshapes the outcome for another. A model that behaves this way produces unreliable decisions no matter how strong its aggregate accuracy looks.

None of this is visible from the prediction alone. The accuracy metrics remain strong and the output appears sound; the dependence on names surfaces only when the model is required to explain how it reached its decision.

Why the Failure Stays Invisible

A conventional classification or regression model that returns only a verdict, such as {"Promotion": "Yes"}, operates as a black box. The output offers no hint that a name tipped the outcome, so the flaw stays hidden until something external drags it into view, and by then the model is already in production, making decisions.

For explainability to be dependable, it has to travel with the prediction itself, produced alongside the result rather than reconstructed after the fact. Responsible AI cannot rest on a verdict that arrives without its reasoning.

SAP RPT 1.5 is built on this principle. The sections that follow examine how it returns an explanation with every prediction.

How SAP RPT 1.5 Enforces Explainability

SAP RPT 1.5, the Relational Prediction Transformer, is a foundation model for tabular and relational data. Given a table with specified cells to predict, it produces predictions in-context, without a per-dataset training run. The characteristic that matters for Responsible AI is architectural: explainability is a first-class field in the API.

RPT 1.5 can be deployed in SAP AI Core and used for inference. The underlying technology is detailed in the ConTextTab research paper published by SAP, with an open-source implementation available as ConTextTab on Hugging Face and GitHub. To try RPT for free and read the FAQs, see the SAP RPT page.

The Request: Asking for the Reasoning Up Front

A prediction is an authenticated REST call to the deployment. Alongside the specification of what to predict, the caller declares which explanation to return, within the prediction_config:

curl --request POST \

  --url $AI_API_URL/v2/inference/deployments/$DEPLOYMENT_ID/predict \

  --header 'ai-resource-group: default' \

  --header 'authorization: Bearer $AUTH_TOKEN' \

  --header 'content-type: application/json' \

  --data '{

  "prediction_config": {

    "target_columns": [

      { "name": "Promotion", "prediction_placeholder": "[PREDICT]", "task_type": "classification", "top_k": 1 }

    ],

    "explanations": {

      "top_column_scores": 4,

      "top_relevant_context_rows": 9

    }

  },

  "rows": [

    { "Name": "Zoey",      "Age": 35, "Gender": "F", "Performance_Rating": 3.5, "Promotion": "[PREDICT]" },

    { "Name": "Alice",     "Age": 34, "Gender": "F", "Performance_Rating": 3.2, "Promotion": "No" },

    { "Name": "Bruce",     "Age": 33, "Gender": "M", "Performance_Rating": 2.5, "Promotion": "No" },

    { "Name": "Catherine", "Age": 35, "Gender": "F", "Performance_Rating": 4.0, "Promotion": "Yes" },

    { "Name": "Donald",    "Age": 32, "Gender": "M", "Performance_Rating": 3.9, "Promotion": "Yes" },

    { "Name": "Eva",       "Age": 33, "Gender": "F", "Performance_Rating": 1.5, "Promotion": "No" },

    { "Name": "Frank",     "Age": 36, "Gender": "M", "Performance_Rating": 1.0, "Promotion": "No" },

    { "Name": "Giselle",   "Age": 35, "Gender": "F", "Performance_Rating": 5.0, "Promotion": "Yes" },

    { "Name": "Henry",     "Age": 38, "Gender": "M", "Performance_Rating": 3.5, "Promotion": "Yes" },

    { "Name": "Zelda",    "Age": 33, "Gender": "F", "Performance_Rating": 3.4, "Promotion": "No" }

  ],

  "data_schema": {

    "Name":               { "dtype": "string" },

    "Age":                { "dtype": "numeric" },

    "Gender":             { "dtype": "string" },

    "Performance_Rating": { "dtype": "numeric" },

    "Promotion":          { "dtype": "string" }

  }

}'

The row to be scored has its target masked with the [PREDICT] placeholder, and the remaining rows serve as in-context evidence.  Because the explanations field is part of the request, every call carries its own justification. Explainability is not a separate job run afterwards; it is produced together with the inference.

The Response: Every Prediction Explains Itself

The response contains the prediction together with the information required to interrogate it:

{
  "explanations": {
    "top_column_scores": [
      {
        "Age": 0.165,
        "Gender": 0.188,
        "Name": 0.331,
        "Performance_Rating": 0.316
      }
    ],
    "top_relevant_context_rows": [
      [ 8, 7, 3, 4, 9, 1, 6, 5, 2 ]
    ]
  },
  "id": "00df0b2c-b93f-4a56-9dc0-c21fd488bc0d",
  "metadata": {
    "num_columns": 5, "num_predictions": 1, "num_query_rows": 1, "num_rows": 10
  },
  "predictions": [
    {
      "Promotion": [
        {
          "confidence": 0.83, "confidence_interval": null, "prediction": "Yes"
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "status": {
    "code": 0,
    "message": "ok"
  }
}

Two elements are returned with the answer:

  1. top_column_scores identifies which features drove the decision:

Feature

Influence

Name

0.331

Performance_Rating

0.316

Gender

0.188

Age

0.165

Name is the most influential feature in the model, ahead of actual job performance and well ahead of Gender and Age.

  1. top_relevant_context_rows identifies which examples the model leaned on. The response names the specific rows (8, 7, 4, 3, and so on) that most shaped the outcome, so a reviewer can inspect the evidence behind a decision instead of taking it on trust.

The effect is straightforward but powerful: a prediction cannot leave RPT 1.5 without the material needed to examine it.

Acting on the Explanation: Removing Columns from the Features

An explanation is only useful if it can be acted upon. Because the column scores identify Name as the feature to remove, the fix is made in the same request contract that surfaced the problem. RPT 1.5 provides an index_column: a parameter used only to identify each row and returned in the response for reference, but never treated as an input feature. For more details on this and other request parameters, refer to the RPT documentation. Designating Name as the index_column takes it out of the model's inputs entirely, without deleting it from the data:

"index_column": "Name",
"explanations": {
    "top_column_scores": 4,
    "top_relevant_context_rows": 9
}

Re-running the identical request with this one change produces a response that confirms the fix:

{
  "explanations": {
    "top_column_scores": [
      {
        "Age": 0.269,
        "Gender": 0.261,
        "Performance_Rating": 0.47
      }
    ],
    "top_relevant_context_rows": [
      [ 8, 7, 3, 4, 9, 1, 6, 5, 2 ]
    ]
  },
  "predictions": [
    {
      "Name": "Zoey",
      "Promotion": [
        { "prediction": "Yes", "confidence": 0.94, "confidence_interval": null }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

The result speaks for itself:

Feature

Influence (before)

Influence (after)

Name

0.331

— (excluded)

Performance_Rating

0.316

0.470

Gender

0.188

0.261

Age

0.165

0.269


Name has disappeared from the scores entirely, and Performance_Rating is now decisively the leading feature at 0.470. The prediction for Zoey holds at Yes, but its confidence rises from 0.83 to 0.94, and Name is echoed back under predictions purely as a row label, no longer as something the model weighed. The decision now rests on the attributes that should drive it, and the same explanation that exposed the flaw is what verifies the correction.

From Detection to Responsible Action

The value of the explanation lies in the actions it enables:

  • Identifying problematic features before deployment. A Name influence of 0.331, the model's top feature, is a signal available on the first call, not after a complaint or an audit. As shown above, the fix is immediate: exclude Name through the index_column and re-run to confirm the model now decides on merit.
  • Auditing individual decisions. When an employee asks why a decision was made, a per-prediction, per-feature explanation already exists to support the response.
  • Establishing trust with the business. Stakeholders can approve what they can understand. A prediction accompanied by its reasoning is one that a decision-maker can stand behind.
  • Governing at scale. Because the explanation is structured data returned with every call, feature-importance drift can be monitored across all predictions and flagged when a model begins relying on a feature it should not.

Conclusion: Explainability by Design, Not by Afterthought

The promotion example is deliberately small, but the lesson scales without limit: a model can be accurate and still be unsafe, and accuracy alone will never tell you which one you have. Only explainability can. That is why explainability is not a feature bolted onto Responsible AI; it is the mechanism that makes Responsible AI verifiable in the first place.

Where explanation is treated as an optional, after-the-fact analysis, it is the first thing to be skipped. SAP RPT 1.5 takes the opposite approach and makes explanation a property of the prediction itself: requested in the contract, returned with the result, and impossible to quietly leave out. When renaming Ivanka to Zelda changes Zoey's outcome, RPT 1.5 does not hide the cause; it surfaces it in the same response, as a feature-importance value that can be acted upon.

A model that explains itself is not merely more transparent. It is the only kind of model that can be deployed with confidence.

entry.title: Data Is More Than a Constant for the AI Engineer
entry.content:
Across decades of computing, the way people built software has changed dramatically, yet one element has remained constant: data. In early IT, programmers encoded logic onto punch cards, stacked them by hand, and fed them into machines that executed business rules one line at a time. A misplaced card could disrupt payroll, inventory, or financial processing because the logic and the data were inseparable in execution. Today, AI engineers are doing so much more than feeding punch cards into mainframes. They are orchestrating large language models, building agents, and connecting systems that can plan, reason, and act on behalf of users. Even with all that change, the dependency underneath remains the same - without a strong data layer, intelligent systems make weak decisions.

Consider both the micro and macro perspectives. At the micro level, an AI engineer is writing code, shaping features, querying patterns, and giving agents access to the right context at the right time. At the macro level, an enterprise is deciding how to structure data so those agents can perform reliably, securely, and at scale. SAP HANA Cloud sits directly in that intersection - it is designed to help AI engineers work with transactional, analytical, and AI data in real time. For teams moving from experimentation to production, recognizing this differentiation matters because the quality of the agent depends not only on the LLM model, but also on the underlying data.

From Linear Programs to Agentic Systems

The punch-card era forced developers to think in fixed sequences. Logic was predefined, the program ran in a linear path, and the output reflected what had already been encoded. Over time, computing became more interactive and more distributed. Database professionals learned to optimize schemas and queries. Full-stack developers built applications across front end, back end, and APIs. Data engineers created pipelines that moved and transformed data continuously. Now AI engineers combine many of those skills in a new pattern: they do not just build software that reacts to commands, but systems that can observe, retrieve, decide, and act in loops.

Agentic AI raises the bar for the data layer. A static application can tolerate latency in ways an autonomous workflow cannot. An agent must retrieve data quickly, reconcile it with prior context, decide what matters, and choose the next action. If the underlying data is fragmented, slow, or spread across too many systems, the agent loses both speed and grounding. If the data layer is responsive, coherent, and able to represent multiple kinds of information, the agent becomes far more useful. SAP HANA Cloud is built for exactly that performance expectation. It combines in-memory speed with support for multiple data models so AI engineers can bring together the structured, semi-structured, and unstructured grounding that agentic workflows need.

 SAP HANA Cloud as the AI Database

SAP HANA Cloud is a fully managed, cloud-native database service designed to deliver high performance, elastic scalability, and advanced analytics for modern enterprise applications. More importantly for this post, it serves as the AI database of the SAP Business AI Platform and as a foundational in-memory, multi-model engine within SAP Business Data Cloud. That positioning is important because AI systems increasingly need a database that does more than store rows and columns. They need a system that can help contextualize, reason, and operationalize multiple types of enterprise data in one place.

For AI engineers, this means the database is no longer just a persistence layer. It becomes part of the reasoning architecture. SAP HANA Cloud supports relational, graph, spatial, JSON, text, and vector data, which gives teams the flexibility to store and work with different forms of business context without forcing every use case into a single rigid shape. A workflow might need order records, geographic coordinates, relationship paths across supply nodes, configuration metadata in JSON, and embeddings that capture behavioral similarity. When those can be handled in one environment, the engineer spends less time stitching systems together and more time building reliable logic on top of trusted enterprise context.

In-Memory Data Storage for Agent Speed

Agentic systems work in loops, and each loop has a time budget. The longer it takes to retrieve and process relevant data, the more brittle the user experience becomes and the less useful the agent feels in practice. SAP HANA Cloud uses in-memory, columnar storage as its primary data layer. That design supports the fast execution of joins, aggregations, and analytical workloads over large data volumes. Instead of repeatedly paging to disk for core workloads, the system is built to operate on active data in memory, which is one reason this database is well suited for scenarios where decisions need to be made quickly.

Consider this analogy. When an experienced colleague can recall the right information immediately, the business process moves forward. When that person must search through binders before every answer, progress slows down and trust in the outcome drops. In agentic AI, the database needs to enable the first scenario. Imagine an agent monitoring unshipped orders and associating them with regional office performance. If that agent waits on slow joins across large transactional tables, every downstream decision is delayed. With SAP HANA Cloud, those joins can run in-memory, allowing AI engineers to embed operational queries into agent workflows without treating the database as a bottleneck.

An example sales order SQL statement:

SELECT
    so.office_id,
    so.office_name,
    o.order_id,
    o.order_status,
    o.shipped_date
FROM sales_office AS so
LEFT OUTER JOIN orders AS o
    ON so.office_id = o.office_id
    AND o.order_status = 'UNSHIPPED'
WHERE so.region = 'NORTH_AMERICA';

This query may look familiar, but the underlying architecture changes the effect. In a slower environment, the database may struggle with searching such a large dataset – even for just reporting purposes. In SAP HANA Cloud, a comprehensive dataset can become part of an agent’s live working memory, allowing the agent to observe open issues, correlate them with known conditions, and decide what to do next.

Multi-Model Data for Simplicity, Not Fragmentation

One of the most practical challenges for AI engineers is not the lack of data, but the number of systems that hold it. Relational databases manage transactions. Search systems handle text. Document stores keep JSON payloads. Graph databases represent relationships. GIS tools support spatial workloads. Vector databases store embeddings. Each of these tools solves a narrow problem well, but the cumulative architecture becomes harder to govern and more difficult to reason over. Every data platform boundary introduces integration work, possible inconsistency, and additional operational overhead.

SAP HANA Cloud addresses this jambalaya of data by providing multi-model support in one database instance. This heterogeneous nature does not mean every use case should be forced into a single data model. It means, however, the engineer has a cohesive environment where multiple representations of business context can “simmer” together. An AI engineer can use relational structures for office and order data, graph representations for logistics routes, spatial coordinates for physical locations, JSON for configuration, and vectors for behavior patterns. Because these data types can be queried together, the database supports a more unified style of reasoning. The result is less semantic fragmentation and more confidence that agents are working from the same “pot” of data.

 As an example, a simple multi-model query that evaluates sales office performance based on a derived machine learning score might look like this:

SELECT
    so.office_id,
    so.office_name,
    ST_AsWKT(so.location)                AS office_location,
    g.path_length                        AS logistics_path_length,
    JSON_VALUE(so.config, '$.priority')  AS priority_flag,
    ml.score                             AS churn_risk_score,
    ve.embedding                         AS office_behavior_vector
FROM sales_office AS so
JOIN logistics_graph AS g
    ON g.source_office = so.office_id
JOIN ml_churn_scores AS ml
    ON ml.office_id = so.office_id
JOIN office_vectors AS ve
    ON ve.office_id = so.office_id
WHERE ST_Within(
    so.location,
    ST_GeomFromText('POLYGON((...))')
)
  AND JSON_VALUE(so.config, '$.active') = true
  AND ml.score > 0.8;

This mutli-model SQL use case is not just a demonstration of flexibility. It illustrates that an agent can receive richer context from a single query and act on it without depending on a group of disparate external systems to reconstruct the same picture.

Higher-Order Intelligence

Similarity is one of the most useful concepts in modern AI. People naturally recognize likeness. However, machines need a more definitive representation of reality. Vectors provide that representation by encoding entities as arrays of numbers that capture meaningful characteristics. SAP HANA Cloud includes a vector engine with native vector types and similarity functions, enabling AI engineers to store embeddings directly alongside business data.

At the micro level, similarity comprehension is powerful because it lets an engineer ask a direct question such as which current offices behave most like an office that previously became problematic. At the macro level, it allows teams to establish pattern recognition based on historical business outcomes and use those patterns to evaluate current behavior. Similarity search now becomes valid for more than just AI grounding – it enables state analysis for any type of use case.

Using Normal Distribution to See Isolated vs Epidemic Problems

While similarity scoring can provide useful context, it does not answer a crucial macro-level question: is a pattern localized or occurring more broadly across the organization? In this blog’s running example, a small number of sales offices with concerning signals may represent localized operational issues, while similar signals across many offices may warrant investigation as a broader pattern. To reason about that distinction, an AI engineer needs more than the determination of similarity to a historical benchmark; they also need a way to measure how unusual the observed behavior is within a defined comparison group and time period.

This type of problem is where augmenting with statistics can help. As an illustrative example, if a KPI such as delayed_order_rate is stable enough and approximately normally distributed for the intended purpose, engineers can standardize each office’s value as a z-score, showing its distance from the reference-group mean in standard-deviation units. Offices within a defined reference band can be treated as typical or low for the KPI, values more than two standard deviations above the mean can be flagged as moderately high, and values more than three standard deviations above the mean can be flagged as exceptionally high. 

Engineers can then count offices in these higher bands and intersect them with offices that have high similarity to a historical risk profile (aka vector), creating a prioritized list for investigation. If only one or two offices meet both conditions in a defined period, the result may indicate a localized pattern. If a larger fraction of offices meet both conditions, particularly across multiple regions or consecutive periods, the result may indicate a broader operational pattern requiring further analysis. Thus, this intersection of micro-level similarity and macro-level statistical analysis gives an AI agent a more grounded basis for deciding what to investigate, escalate, or recommend next.

Putting Data to Work

This blog post demonstrates how AI engineers can utilize the data layer to ground AI with business context. Engineers need a database that can handle operational queries, multiple data models, similarity reasoning, and pattern recognition without creating unnecessary complexity. SAP HANA Cloud supports the engineer by bringing those capabilities into the same environment. Ultimately, true business impact can be found in a more grounded, coherent system where data, context, and reasoning stay connected.

Whether you remember days of hand coding logic, work daily with billions of rows, or ground AI agents with the knowledge to make independent decisions, the data underneath those solutions continues to become more valuable with every use case. For the AI engineer, this utility means data is more than just a constant. Data as business context is an asset that can multiply its value tremendously over time.

Try for Yourself

The SAP HANA Cloud basic trial is a great learning experience that promotes hands-on with many of the concepts mentioned in this blog. The included tutorial explains database setup, tooling, and offers a starter scenario. After that, you can reuse the same basic trial environment to load the example script at the end of this post. Completing these two activities lets you see first-hand how the same SAP HANA Cloud database can be used for analytics, applications, and AI.

When you are ready to prove out a real use case, consider deploying an SAP HANA Cloud free tier instance. The free tier option gives you more control over configuration and a path from evaluation to productive usage without starting from scratch.

Example Script with Sample Data

Note the you may need to set the schema before running this script.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- END-TO-END: VECTOR SIMILARITY + PREDICTIVE SCORING + DERIVED HIGH-BAND FLAG
-- SAP HANA CLOUD
-- Use Case: Identify the sales offices that resemble a benchmark for a problematic office.
-- Note for simplicity, transactional aggregations have already occurred before these steps
--
-- DESIGN:
-- - Base table: KPIs + REAL_VECTOR embeddings
-- - Similarity: COSINE_SIMILARITY(behavior_vector, TO_REAL_VECTOR(...))
-- - predicted_risk_score: similarity + KPI blend
-- - risk_band: derived from predicted_risk_score
-- - is_problematic: derived from risk_band = 'high'
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 0) CLEANUP (SAFE TO RUN MULTIPLE TIMES)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DROP VIEW  office_final_results;
DROP VIEW  office_risk_bands;
DROP VIEW  office_risk_predictions;
DROP VIEW  office_similarity_features;
DROP TABLE office_risk_profile;

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 1) BASE TABLE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE COLUMN TABLE office_risk_profile (
    office_id                 NVARCHAR(40) PRIMARY KEY,
    region                    NVARCHAR(40),
    office_name               NVARCHAR(120),
    delayed_order_rate        DOUBLE,
    return_rate               DOUBLE,
    service_ticket_rate       DOUBLE,
    revenue_volatility        DOUBLE,
    employee_turnover_rate    DOUBLE,
    behavior_vector           REAL_VECTOR(8)
);

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 2) SAMPLE DATA
-- OFF001, OFF002, OFF005: intended high
-- OFF003: intended moderate
-- OFF004, OFF006, OFF007, OFF008: intended low
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
INSERT INTO office_risk_profile VALUES
('OFF001','NORTH_AMERICA','Chicago Central', 0.46,0.19,0.35,0.29,0.22,
 TO_REAL_VECTOR('[0.95,0.87,0.81,0.73,0.61,0.43,0.36,0.25]'));

INSERT INTO office_risk_profile VALUES
('OFF002','NORTH_AMERICA','Dallas Hub',      0.43,0.18,0.33,0.27,0.21,
 TO_REAL_VECTOR('[0.92,0.84,0.78,0.70,0.59,0.42,0.35,0.24]'));

INSERT INTO office_risk_profile VALUES
('OFF003','NORTH_AMERICA','Denver West',     0.27,0.11,0.21,0.18,0.14,
 TO_REAL_VECTOR('[0.68,0.61,0.55,0.49,0.41,0.29,0.23,0.16]'));

INSERT INTO office_risk_profile VALUES
('OFF004','NORTH_AMERICA','Boston East',     0.08,0.03,0.07,0.07,0.05,
 TO_REAL_VECTOR('[0.07,0.12,0.18,0.24,0.31,0.39,0.46,0.54]'));

INSERT INTO office_risk_profile VALUES
('OFF005','EUROPE','Berlin Core',            0.41,0.17,0.31,0.25,0.20,
 TO_REAL_VECTOR('[0.90,0.82,0.76,0.68,0.57,0.41,0.34,0.23]'));

INSERT INTO office_risk_profile VALUES
('OFF006','EUROPE','Paris South',            0.09,0.03,0.08,0.07,0.05,
 TO_REAL_VECTOR('[0.05,0.10,0.16,0.22,0.30,0.38,0.47,0.56]'));

INSERT INTO office_risk_profile VALUES
('OFF007','APJ','Singapore One',             0.09,0.03,0.08,0.07,0.05,
 TO_REAL_VECTOR('[0.09,0.14,0.20,0.27,0.35,0.44,0.53,0.62]'));

INSERT INTO office_risk_profile VALUES
('OFF008','APJ','Sydney Metro',              0.10,0.04,0.08,0.07,0.05,
 TO_REAL_VECTOR('[0.06,0.11,0.17,0.25,0.34,0.45,0.57,0.69]'));

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 3) VECTOR SIMILARITY FEATURES
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE VIEW office_similarity_features AS
SELECT
    o.office_id,
    o.region,
    o.office_name,
    o.delayed_order_rate,
    o.return_rate,
    o.service_ticket_rate,
    o.revenue_volatility,
    o.employee_turnover_rate,
    COSINE_SIMILARITY(
        o.behavior_vector,
        TO_REAL_VECTOR('[0.91,0.83,0.77,0.69,0.58,0.41,0.35,0.23]')
    ) AS problem_similarity
FROM office_risk_profile AS o;

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 4) NORMALITY CHECK FOR delayed_order_rate
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
WITH stats AS (
    SELECT
        AVG(delayed_order_rate)        AS mean_dor,
        STDDEV_POP(delayed_order_rate) AS std_dor
    FROM office_risk_profile
),
z_scores AS (
    SELECT
        o.office_id,
        o.office_name,
        o.region,
        o.delayed_order_rate,
        (o.delayed_order_rate - stats.mean_dor) / NULLIF(stats.std_dor, 0) AS z_dor
    FROM office_risk_profile AS o
    CROSS JOIN stats
),
coverage AS (
    SELECT
        COUNT(*) AS n,
        SUM(CASE WHEN ABS(z_dor) <= 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS n_within_1sd,
        SUM(CASE WHEN ABS(z_dor) <= 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS n_within_2sd,
        SUM(CASE WHEN ABS(z_dor) <= 3 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS n_within_3sd
    FROM z_scores
),
shape AS (
    SELECT
        n,
        n_within_1sd,
        n_within_2sd,
        n_within_3sd,
        n_within_1sd * 1.0 / n AS pct_within_1sd,
        n_within_2sd * 1.0 / n AS pct_within_2sd,
        n_within_3sd * 1.0 / n AS pct_within_3sd
    FROM coverage
)
SELECT
    n,
    pct_within_1sd,
    pct_within_2sd,
    pct_within_3sd,
    CASE
        WHEN pct_within_1sd BETWEEN 0.50 AND 0.85
         AND pct_within_2sd BETWEEN 0.85 AND 1.00
         AND pct_within_3sd >= 0.95
        THEN 'approximately_normal_under_symmetry_assumption'
        ELSE 'non_normal_under_symmetry_assumption'
    END AS delayed_order_rate_normality_flag
FROM shape;

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 5) CLASSIFY OFFICES INTO STANDARD-DEVIATION BANDS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
WITH stats AS (
    SELECT
        AVG(delayed_order_rate)        AS mean_dor,
        STDDEV_POP(delayed_order_rate) AS std_dor
    FROM office_risk_profile
),
z_scores AS (
    SELECT
        o.office_id,
        o.office_name,
        o.region,
        o.delayed_order_rate,
        (o.delayed_order_rate - stats.mean_dor) / NULLIF(stats.std_dor, 0) AS z_dor
    FROM office_risk_profile AS o
    CROSS JOIN stats
),
classified AS (
    SELECT
        office_id,
        office_name,
        region,
        delayed_order_rate,
        z_dor,
        CASE
            WHEN z_dor >= 3 THEN 'extreme_high'
            WHEN z_dor >= 2 THEN 'moderate_high'
            WHEN z_dor <= -3 THEN 'extreme_low'
            WHEN z_dor <= -2 THEN 'moderate_low'
            ELSE 'normal'
        END AS dor_band
    FROM z_scores
)
SELECT
    dor_band,
    COUNT(*) AS office_count
FROM classified
GROUP BY dor_band
ORDER BY dor_band;

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 6) INTERSECT SD BANDS WITH HIGH VECTOR SIMILARITY (DIAGNOSTIC)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
WITH high_similarity AS (
    SELECT
        office_id,
        problem_similarity
    FROM office_similarity_features
    WHERE problem_similarity >= 0.8
),
stats AS (
    SELECT
        AVG(delayed_order_rate)        AS mean_dor,
        STDDEV_POP(delayed_order_rate) AS std_dor
    FROM office_risk_profile
),
z_scores AS (
    SELECT
        o.office_id,
        o.office_name,
        o.region,
        o.delayed_order_rate,
        (o.delayed_order_rate - stats.mean_dor) / NULLIF(stats.std_dor, 0) AS z_dor
    FROM office_risk_profile AS o
    CROSS JOIN stats
),
classified AS (
    SELECT
        office_id,
        office_name,
        region,
        delayed_order_rate,
        z_dor,
        CASE
            WHEN z_dor >= 3 THEN 'extreme_high'
            WHEN z_dor >= 2 THEN 'moderate_high'
            WHEN z_dor <= -3 THEN 'extreme_low'
            WHEN z_dor <= -2 THEN 'moderate_low'
            ELSE 'normal'
        END AS dor_band
    FROM z_scores
)
SELECT
    c.dor_band,
    COUNT(*) AS high_risk_office_count
FROM classified AS c
JOIN high_similarity AS h
    ON c.office_id = h.office_id
GROUP BY c.dor_band
ORDER BY c.dor_band;

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 7) PREDICTIVE SCORING VIEW
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE VIEW office_risk_predictions AS
SELECT
    office_id,
    region,
    office_name,
    delayed_order_rate,
    return_rate,
    service_ticket_rate,
    revenue_volatility,
    employee_turnover_rate,
    problem_similarity,
    (
        0.62 * problem_similarity +
        0.15 * delayed_order_rate +
        0.10 * return_rate +
        0.08 * service_ticket_rate +
        0.03 * revenue_volatility +
        0.02 * employee_turnover_rate
    ) AS predicted_risk_score
FROM office_similarity_features;

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 8) RISK BAND VIEW
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE VIEW office_risk_bands AS
SELECT
    office_id,
    region,
    office_name,
    predicted_risk_score,
    CASE
        WHEN predicted_risk_score >= 0.70 THEN 'high'
        WHEN predicted_risk_score >= 0.45 THEN 'moderate'
        ELSE 'low'
    END AS risk_band
FROM office_risk_predictions;

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 9) FINAL RESULTS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE VIEW office_final_results AS
SELECT
    p.office_id,
    p.office_name,
    p.region,
    ROUND(p.problem_similarity, 4)   AS problem_similarity,
    ROUND(p.predicted_risk_score, 4) AS predicted_risk_score,
    b.risk_band,
    CASE
        WHEN b.risk_band = 'high' THEN 1
        ELSE 0
    END AS is_problematic
FROM office_risk_predictions AS p
JOIN office_risk_bands       AS b
    ON p.office_id = b.office_id;

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 10) FINAL OUTPUT
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SELECT
    office_id,
    office_name,
    region,
    problem_similarity,
    predicted_risk_score,
    risk_band,
    is_problematic
FROM office_final_results
ORDER BY predicted_risk_score DESC;

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 11) SUMMARY COUNTS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SELECT
    risk_band,
    COUNT(*) AS office_count
FROM office_final_results
GROUP BY risk_band
ORDER BY
    CASE risk_band
        WHEN 'high' THEN 1
        WHEN 'moderate' THEN 2
        WHEN 'low'      THEN 3
        ELSE 4
    END;

entry.title: Your AI Agent Can Talk to SAP HR. Practical Demo available here | Part - 1
entry.content:
Part 1 of 2 story first, architecture second. Audience: SuccessFactors Specialist, SAP Architects and AI enthusiastic .

Background Story:

It started with a simple question.

"Tell me about Sarah and her professional journey with our organization. Is she a good fit for the next level of promotion?"

That's it. No forms. No filters. No five screens to track down one person.

Joule reached for its built-in tools, SFSF deep-links enabled, and after a long search came back with an answer,  but one that still left a lot to be desired, because its skills around SFSF are limited to say about Sarah.

Meiyazhagan, an SAP SuccessFactors Specialist, saw room to close that gap with MCP,  so any agent could connect to SFSF and return better results.

We built MCP tools for SFSF (17 tools) that let a model understand your employees properly, because out of the box, it couldn't.

Credits: Illustration generated with Gemini

Here's the Thing Nobody Outside the Integration Team Understands

Joule or Claude does not speak OData.

That sentence sounds too small to be the problem. It is the whole problem.

A business user will never type GET /odata/v2/User?$filter=department eq 'Finance'&$select=userId,firstName,lastName,managerId. They will ask Joule, or Claude. The agent has to choose a tool, pass typed arguments, survive a 401, and come back with a sentence a manager can use in a 1:1.

SuccessFactors, for its part, does not speak MCP. It speaks OData v2, company-id scoped tokens, and Role-Based Permissions that were designed for human users in a browser not for a FastMCP process sitting on BTP calling on behalf of Joule. Here you can try our custom build tools from huggingFace (for demo purpose only, dont use in production)

  • App LandingPage: https://huggingface.co/spaces/HeisenbergLupenix/SuccessFactors_MCP
  • MCP Landing Page: https://heisenberglupenix-successfactors-mcp.hf.space/

So every landscape walk into has invented some version of the same gap-filler:

  • A consultant pastes a company password into chat "just for the pilot."
  • A CAP service that wraps three entities and dies on the fourth.
  • An Integration Suite iFlow that was meant to be temporary.
  • HTTP Basic (username at company) on a technical user, even though SAP retires Basic authentication for SuccessFactors APIs on 20 November 2026 (KBA 3472405).

None of those are the last mile. They are workarounds around the last mile.

The Tenant Already Knows the Employee. Just Not in a Shape the Agent Can Touch.

Take the question from the demo.

Find employees in Finance reporting to Jane.

Employee Central already has this. User has the people. department or FODepartment has Finance. manager / managerId has the reporting line. If Jane is only a name, search against User resolves her to a userId. Then User filtered by that manager id returns the team.

What the agent does not have:

  1. A stable way to say "search" versus "get one" versus "walk the org."
  2. A token that belongs to this company, not the sandbox from the last workshop.
  3. A refusal path when the caller is a manager who should see direct reports and nothing else especially not someone else's EmpCompensation.
  4. An error it can recover from. "HTTP 404" is not a hint. "Employee 100999 was not found. If you only have a name, call search_employee first" is a hint.

That fourth one is the quiet killer. Architects design the happy path. Agents live on the unhappy path. They retry the same userId, they invent a compensation number, they ask the human for a password. If the tool JSON is not written for the agent, the agent will do all three.

The agent does not need to predict who Jane is. It needs a tool that searches, a tool that fetches, and a runtime that will not return pay data unless the user asked and the caller is allowed.

Connect the Sandbox SFSF from SAP Hub using api keys:

  • Enter the Test Sandbox API key from SAP Hub
  • Click Test connection for testing

Link: https://heisenberglupenix-successfactors-mcp.hf.space/connect

What Actually Put in the Path

Clients stay where they already are. Joule, Claude, Cursor, VS Code. SuccessFactors MCP is not a chatbot. It owns the last mile:

HR question
  → MCP client (Joule / Claude / Cursor)
    → HTTPS POST /mcp   or   stdio
      → tenant middleware (API key, request id, rate limit, audit)
        → READ tool
          → scope check  →  caller scoping (self / manager / admin)
            → OAuth token cache (this tenant only)
              → GET /odata/v2/...
                → JSON the agent can narrate

Three backends, one contract:

HTTP Basic is not on the connect form. It is not coming back.

The Tools Are Named for the Question, Not for the Entity

This is the part consultants get wrong when they wrap OData 1:1.

The agent should not have to know that "who do they report to" is User.manager. It should see get_manager. The catalog in this release is READ only:

The human asks The agent should call SuccessFactors with our custom tool from:

https://heisenberglupenix-successfactors-mcp.hf.space/tools

 

Find people in Finance

How do I reach them?

Profile + job + talent probes, no compensation

tell_my_story is the human half of the exit-interview thread. The exit interview already knew who was leaving. This tool is what the record looks like while they are still here: goals, reviews, skills, learning, achievements, folded into a career_context plus a story_brief. The MCP server does not write the prose. The LLM does. The server refuses to smuggle EmpCompensation into a "tell me about myself" payload, because that is how pay data leaks into a career narrative nobody asked to classify.

Add MCP server in Joule/Claude/VSCode or any agentic platform:

Go to Claude -> Click + icon -> Manage Connector -> Add Connector 

  • Name: SFSF
  • URL: https://heisenberglupenix-successfactors-mcp.hf.space/mcp

Then Click -> Connect. It will redirect to the below page. 

Write tools are on the roadmap. When they arrive they will require confirm=true after the user explicitly agrees. Agents do not silently PATCH Employee Central. If you have seen a demo where they do, that demo is not ready for your tenant.

After Click Connect from Claude. You can see the below options:

Select the demo employee -> Click Continue as the employee. 

After successful connection to our MCP tool:

Try this prompts:

Isolation Is Not a Slide. It Is the Product.

One admin key from /connect can read any employee in that company. That is correct for the one HR admin who owns the connection. It is wrong to hand to every people manager in the landscape.

For a real OAuth tenant, the server issues caller-scoped keys:

  • self - own userId only.
  • manager - own record plus direct reports. Not the full subtree. Not a skip-level fishing expedition.
  • Compensation for anyone else still needs the admin key, even if they report to you.

Demo and API Hub sandbox skip this panel. There is no real PII behind them. Production does not skip it.

Secrets sit in Fernet-encrypted blobs. Tokens never appear in MCP JSON, logs, or the UI after save. Audit lines carry request_id, tenant id, tool name, status, duration not the employee row. Rate limits sit on /mcp. Timeouts come back as a sentence the agent can say out loud:

The SuccessFactors API request timed out. Please try again.

If you cannot put that sentence in front of a works council, the design is not finished.

This Is Not Joule. This Is What Joule Was Missing.

We have no interest in replacing Joule, or SuccessFactors, or IAS.

Joule Studio or Claude or Gemini wants Streamable HTTP at https://<host>/mcp. It does not want stdio. It does not want the old SSE transport. It does not run a browser OAuth dance inside the chat. Credentials live on the MCP process (or on a destination that process uses). One dedicated deployment maps to one company id. That is the tenant-isolation boundary Joule actually expects in production.

The user types the question. The trace should show search_employee(department="Finance"). The JSON should say "ok": true. It should never contain access_token, apikey, or a password.

That is the space this fills: not a capture tool, not a three-way match engine, not an attrition model, not a new digital assistant.

Now ask the right question in natural language to get the results like:

Just the component that lets the agent ask the tenant that already knows.
