entry.title: Beyond SAP Snowflake ML: Calling SAP HANA Cloud ML and RPT-1.5 via External Access Integration (EAI)
entry.content:
SAP Snowflake has been available in the SAP Business Data Cloud (BDC) as a Solution Extension for a few months now. In the first post of this series, we built our first ML model natively, using Snowflake's own ML capabilities together with Cortex AI. But what if we want to go beyond that and also leverage SAP's existing AI offerings, such as SAP HANA Cloud's ML capabilities (PAL/APL) and the RPT-1.5 model from Generative AI Hub — all from the same Snowflake Notebook? That's exactly what we'll set up in this hands-on tutorial.

Here we'll wire up an External Access Integration (EAI) so a Snowflake Notebook can securely call two SAP services over the network:

  1. SAP HANA Cloud - connect and run SQL / ML (PAL/APL) remotely.
  2. SAP-RPT-1.5 via Generative AI Hub - the relational foundation model for tabular prediction.

Everything stays governed: credentials live in Snowflake secrets (encrypted at rest), egress is locked down to named hosts via network rules, and access is granted to a single role.

Table of contents

  • Architecture: how External Access Integration (EAI) fits
  • Prerequisites
  • Understanding the building blocks
  • Step 1 - Run the setup SQL
  • Step 2 - Attach the integration & secrets to the notebook
  • Step 3 - Verify from the notebook
  • Step 4 - Connect to SAP HANA Cloud
  • Step 5 - Call the Generative AI Hub
  • Step 6 - Predict with SAP RPT-1.5
  • Troubleshooting
  • Conclusion & Next Steps

Architecture: how External Access Integration (EAI) fits

By default, code running in SAP Snowflake cannot make arbitrary outbound network calls - that's a good security default. An External Access Integration is the account-level object that selectively opens that door. It binds together two kinds of schema-level objects:

  • Network rules - an allowlist of exact host:port destinations for egress.
  • Secrets - encrypted credentials your code reads at runtime.

Once the integration is attached to a notebook's connected service, the notebook can reach the allowed hosts and read the allowed secrets - nothing more.

Prerequisites

  • Access to SAP Business Data Cloud with the Snowflake Solution Extension enabled.
  • The ACCOUNTADMIN role in Snowflake (to create the integration, network rules and secrets).
  • An SAP AI Core service key with a deployed LLM and RPT-1.5 model.
  • SAP HANA Cloud credentials - host, port, user, password.
  • Basic familiarity with SQL and Python.
⚠️Security first. The setup script stores real credentials. Keep the filled-in copy local, never commit it, and rotate the AI Core client secret and HANA password if they are ever exposed. In this blog every credential is shown as a <PLACEHOLDER>.

Understanding the building blocks

Three Snowflake objects work together:

ObjectScopePurpose
NETWORK RULESchemaAllowlist of host:port egress destinations (no wildcards - hosts are matched literally).
SECRETSchemaCredential encrypted at rest. Not even ACCOUNTADMIN can SELECT it; code reads it via the secrets API.
EXTERNAL ACCESS INTEGRATIONAccountBinds the rules + secrets and is attached to a notebook's connected service.

 

💡Network rules and secrets are schema-level, so they need a home. We use a dedicated SAP_INTEGRATION.CONFIG schema to keep them tidy - but your notebook can still run in any database.

Step 1 - Run the setup SQL

Run the following as ACCOUNTADMIN. Here are the key parts.

1a. Create a home for the objects

USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS SAP_INTEGRATION;
CREATE SCHEMA   IF NOT EXISTS SAP_INTEGRATION.CONFIG;
USE DATABASE SAP_INTEGRATION;
USE SCHEMA   CONFIG;

1b. Network rules (egress allowlist)

CREATE OR REPLACE NETWORK RULE aicore_network_rule
  MODE = EGRESS
  TYPE = HOST_PORT
  VALUE_LIST = (
    '<AICORE_AUTH_HOST>',   -- OAuth token server
    '<AICORE_API_HOST>',    -- AI API endpoint
    'ml.hana.ondemand.com'   -- inference deployment domain
  );

CREATE OR REPLACE NETWORK RULE hana_network_rule
  MODE = EGRESS
  TYPE = HOST_PORT
  VALUE_LIST = ( '<HANA_HOST>:443' );
💡Get the host values straight from your AI Core service key: the auth host is the host part of url, and the API host is the host part of serviceurls.AI_API_URL.

1c. Secrets (encrypted at rest)

CREATE OR REPLACE SECRET aicore_secret
  TYPE = GENERIC_STRING
  SECRET_STRING = '{
  "serviceurls": { "AI_API_URL": "<AI_API_URL>" },
  "clientid": "<CLIENT_ID>",
  "clientsecret": "<CLIENT_SECRET>",
  "url": "<AUTH_URL>"
}';

CREATE OR REPLACE SECRET hana_secret
  TYPE = GENERIC_STRING
  SECRET_STRING = '{
  "address": "<HANA_HOST>",
  "port": 443,
  "user": "<HANA_USER>",
  "password": "<HANA_PASSWORD>"
}';

1d. Bind everything into one integration

CREATE OR REPLACE EXTERNAL ACCESS INTEGRATION sap_external_access_integration
  ALLOWED_NETWORK_RULES          = (aicore_network_rule, hana_network_rule)
  ALLOWED_AUTHENTICATION_SECRETS = (aicore_secret, hana_secret)
  ENABLED = TRUE;

1e. Grant to a role

CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS DATA_SCIENTIST;
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE SAP_INTEGRATION       TO ROLE DATA_SCIENTIST;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA   SAP_INTEGRATION.CONFIG TO ROLE DATA_SCIENTIST;
GRANT USAGE ON INTEGRATION sap_external_access_integration TO ROLE DATA_SCIENTIST;
GRANT READ  ON SECRET aicore_secret TO ROLE DATA_SCIENTIST;
GRANT READ  ON SECRET hana_secret   TO ROLE DATA_SCIENTIST;

You can also run all of the SQL snippets together in a single execution.

 

 

Step 2 - Attach the integration & secrets to the notebook

Create a Snowflake Notebook (Projects → Workspaces → + Notebook) and switch its role to DATA_SCIENTIST (make sure to add the newly created role to your user before). Then open the notebook's connected service settings and, under External access, enable sap_external_access_integration and attach both secrets (aicore_secret, hana_secret).

 

 

Step 3 - Verify from the notebook

A quick sanity check that the role is right and the objects are visible, then load the secrets at runtime:

SELECT CURRENT_ROLE();
SHOW EXTERNAL ACCESS INTEGRATIONS LIKE 'sap_external_access_integration';
SHOW NETWORK RULES IN SCHEMA SAP_INTEGRATION.CONFIG;

In a SQL cell of a Snowflake Notebook, only the last statement's result is displayed. To see results from all three, you need to put each statement in its own cell.


Next, we verify that the Snowflake Notebook can access the secrets created in the previous step. The secret values are retrieved securely at runtime and parsed as JSON. To avoid exposing sensitive information, we only print non-sensitive connection details such as the AI API URL and the SAP HANA Cloud host.

import json
from snowflake.snowpark.secrets import get_generic_secret_string

aicore_cfg = json.loads(get_generic_secret_string('sap_integration/config/aicore_secret'))
hana_cfg   = json.loads(get_generic_secret_string('sap_integration/config/hana_secret'))
print("AI API URL:", aicore_cfg["serviceurls"]["AI_API_URL"])
print("HANA host :", hana_cfg["address"])
💡The secret path is database/schema/secret_name (case-insensitive). Secrets are read into memory only - nothing is printed to the cell output.

 

Step 4 - Connect to SAP HANA Cloud

Before connecting to SAP HANA Cloud, we need to install the hana-ml python package with a dedicated cell.

%pip install hana-ml

With the credentials in hand, we can now open a hana-ml connection and confirm the version:

import hana_ml.dataframe as dataframe

conn = dataframe.ConnectionContext(
    address=hana_cfg["address"],
    port=hana_cfg["port"],
    user=hana_cfg["user"],
    password=hana_cfg["password"],
)
print("Connected:", conn.connection.isconnected())
print("HANA version:", conn.hana_version())
💡If HANA Cloud filters inbound traffic by IP, print the notebook's egress IP first (requests.get('https://api.ipify.org').text) and add it to the HANA Cloud allowlist. Tip: Snowflake's AI copilot (CoCo) can generate this snippet for you.

 

 

Step 5 - Call the Generative AI Hub

Again, before connecting to the Generative AI Hub, we need to install the sap-ai-sdk-gen python package with a dedicated cell.

%pip install sap-ai-sdk-gen

The sap-ai-sdk-gen python package reads AICORE_* environment variables. Map them from the secret, then prompt a deployed model:

import os
os.environ["AICORE_AUTH_URL"]       = aicore_cfg["url"]
os.environ["AICORE_CLIENT_ID"]      = aicore_cfg["clientid"]
os.environ["AICORE_CLIENT_SECRET"]  = aicore_cfg["clientsecret"]
os.environ["AICORE_BASE_URL"]       = aicore_cfg["serviceurls"]["AI_API_URL"]
os.environ["AICORE_RESOURCE_GROUP"] = "default"

from gen_ai_hub.proxy.native.openai import responses
response = responses.create(
    model="gpt-5",
    instructions="You are a helpful assistant.",
    input="What is the capital of France?",
)
print(response.output_text)

 

Step 6 - Predict with SAP RPT-1.5

RPT-1.5 is SAP's relational foundation model for tabular data. We call its predict endpoint directly with an OAuth token. First, resolve the host so you can confirm it's covered by the network rule:

from urllib.parse import urlparse
DEPLOYMENT_ID = "<YOUR_DEPLOYMENT_ID>"
API_URL = f'{aicore_cfg["serviceurls"]["AI_API_URL"]}/v2/inference/deployments/{DEPLOYMENT_ID}/predict'
print("Predict host:", urlparse(API_URL).hostname)

Then set up a payload which you can later on change for your own specific use case.

payload = {
    "index_column": "id",
    "prediction_config": {
        "target_columns": [
            {
                "name": "category",
                "prediction_placeholder": "?",
                "task_type": "classification",
                "top_k": 1,
            }
        ],
        "explanations": {"top_column_scores": 4, "top_relevant_context_rows": 3},
    },
    "parse_data_types": "true",
    "data_schema": {
        "id": {"dtype": "numeric"},
        "product": {"dtype": "string"},
        "price": {"dtype": "numeric"},
        "category": {"dtype": "string"},
        "stock": {"dtype": "numeric"},
        "production_date": {"dtype": "date"},
    },
    "rows": [
        {"id": 1, "product": "Laptop", "price": 899, "category": "Electronics", "stock": "150", "production_date": "2024-01-15"},
        {"id": 2, "product": "Mouse", "price": 25, "category": "Accessories", "stock": "500", "production_date": "2024-02-20"},
        {"id": 3, "product": "Keyboard", "price": 75, "category": "Accessories", "stock": "320", "production_date": "2024-03-10"},
        {"id": 4, "product": "Monitor", "price": 350, "category": "?", "stock": "200", "production_date": "2024-03-25"},
    ],
}

And lastly, fetch a token and send the tabular payload (predicting the missing category for the last row):

import requests
def get_access_token():
    data = {"grant_type": "client_credentials",
            "client_id": aicore_cfg["clientid"],
            "client_secret": aicore_cfg["clientsecret"]}
    r = requests.post(aicore_cfg["url"] + "/oauth/token", data=data,
                      headers={"Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"})
    return r.json()["access_token"]

token = get_access_token()
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}", "AI-Resource-Group": "default"}
result = requests.post(API_URL, headers=headers, json=payload).json()
print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))

 

Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely cause & fix
Egress / network errorTarget host not in a network rule - add it and re-run the CREATE OR REPLACE NETWORK RULE.
Secret not foundWrong role, secret not attached to the connected service, or wrong db/schema/name path.
401 / OAuth errorClient id/secret expired - rotate the AI Core service key and update aicore_secret.
HANA connection refusedAdd the notebook's egress IP to the HANA Cloud allowlist.

Conclusion & Next Steps

With a single External Access Integration we've securely reached two SAP services - SAP HANA Cloud and Generative AI Hub including RPT-1.5 - from a governed SAP Snowflake notebook. Credentials stayed encrypted, egress stayed locked down, and access was scoped to one role.

From here you can combine these capabilities: pull features from HANA Cloud, enrich them with an LLM, score them with RPT-1.5, and write results back into the SAP landscape.

What's coming next in this series

  • Building Streamlit apps directly in SAP Snowflake.
  • From SAP-managed to custom-managed Data Products - and sharing them back.

Connect with me on LinkedIn to get notified when the next post goes live. Now it's your turn - which SAP AI service would you wire up first? Happy building! 🦾

entry.title: The next task is easy to find. The next best move is the real warehouse execution challenge.
entry.content:
The Next Task Is Not the Best Task

Toward EWM Next-Best-Move Orchestration

SAP EWM has become very good at managing warehouse tasks. Warehouse orders, queues, resource management, and task interleaving already reduce travel and improve execution efficiency.

But warehouses don't operate under static conditions.

In real operations, conditions change constantly: a forklift finishes putaway, a truck arrives early, another truck is delayed, a replenishment becomes critical, a forklift battery drops, and an urgent order starts to risk missing its SLA.

The warehouse changes every minute. So why should task sequencing stay relatively static between planning cycles?

That question is the starting point for this post: an idea I'll call EWM Next-Best-Move Orchestration - a layer that continuously evaluates warehouse state, resource capability, and transportation events to recommend the highest-value physical move at each moment, not just the nearest one.

This Isn't Entirely New - And That's Worth Saying Upfront

Before going further, it's worth being upfront about something: this direction is no longer purely conceptual. At SAP Sapphire 2026, SAP introduced Autonomous Supply Chain Management, which includes an EWM Real-Time Optimization Agent that continuously re-sequences warehouse tasks as conditions change, and a Joule Logistics Assistant that coordinates warehouse and transportation execution instead of waiting for manual handoffs. SAP also launched SAP Logistics Management as a cloud-native option for warehouses that don't need the full scope of EWM.

So the core idea here - continuous, value-based re-sequencing instead of static planning - lines up with where SAP has publicly said it's heading, and early capability already exists. What I want to add in this post is a more concrete evaluation model, a decision-loop framing, a worked example, and a few governance and readiness questions that tend to get skipped in roadmap slides.

From Task Assignment to Next-Best-Move

Traditional execution can be simplified as:

Order → Warehouse Task → Queue → Resource → Execution

SAP EWM task interleaving already improves on this by assigning a suitable follow-on task instead of sending the resource back empty. The next evolution isn't asking “what task is closest?” It's asking, “given everything happening in the warehouse right now, what action creates the highest operational value?”

That's a genuinely different problem - it means combining signals that today usually live in separate systems.

What Would the Agent Actually Evaluate?

Four live dimensions, combined continuously:

  1. Operator and equipment position. Where is the resource right now? Real-time location data (RTLS) gives the current physical position. A forklift finishing putaway in Aisle 18 shouldn't automatically get sent across the warehouse if valuable work is available nearby - but proximity alone isn't enough to decide.
  2. Equipment capability. Forklift type, load capacity, high-rack capability, operator qualification, battery condition, current equipment status. The question shifts from “who's available?” to “who's capable, available, and best positioned?”
  3. Dock and transportation status. This is where it goes beyond traditional interleaving. Picture two outbound trucks: Truck A is delayed 30 minutes; Truck B is already at the dock, waiting on 10 pallets. A static priority sequence has no way to notice that Truck B just became the higher-risk truck. A value-based layer can recognize that shift and elevate the associated tasks - turning a transportation event into a warehouse execution decision.
  4. Task interleaving, with a value lens. A forklift finishes putaway. Three options exist: a pick 100m away, a replenishment 80m away that unblocks 12 other picks, or an urgent outbound task 150m away that would otherwise miss its departure window. The closest task isn't necessarily the most valuable one. The goal isn't minimizing distance - it's maximizing operational value.

A Quick Example

It's 10:17 AM. A forklift just finished putaway in Aisle 18. There are 40+ open tasks. The system sees:

  • An outbound truck waiting at Door 14
  • 11 picks blocked by one pending replenishment
  • Another carrier delayed by 35 minutes
  • Forklift F07 positioned near the replenishment, with the right equipment capability

Instead of grabbing the nearest task, the logic recognizes a chain: replenishment → unlocks 11 picks → supports the waiting truck → reduces SLA risk. The recommended sequence becomes:

Putaway → Replenishment → Outbound Pick → Staging → Dock

The forklift hasn't just completed tasks - it's executed a chain of operational value a distance-based rule would have missed entirely.

The Decision Loop Behind It

Operationally, this runs as a loop: Detect → Understand → Decide → Act → Learn.

  • Detect - pull signals from SAP EWM, RTLS, IoT/equipment telemetry, Yard/TM, and RF devices.
  • Understand - assemble a live picture: open tasks, resource positions, equipment status, order priorities, dock conditions, SLA risk, dependencies.
  • Decide - apply value-based logic (as in the example above) to determine what should happen next, who should do it, and which sequence creates the most value.
  • Act - push the instruction to the worker, RF device, forklift, AMR, or automation layer.
  • Learn - measure the outcome and feed it back into the next decision.

The result is a continuous execution loop rather than a sequence set once and run until the next planning cycle.

More Than “AI in WMS”

The market is already talking about agentic AI in warehouse management, so just saying “AI can dynamically assign tasks” isn't differentiated on its own. The more interesting question is: what exactly is the AI optimizing?

The answer here is specific: not the next task, not the shortest distance, not resource utilization in isolation - but the next physical move of the warehouse, the action that creates the greatest combined operational value at that moment.

Where SAP BTP Fits

This doesn't require replacing SAP EWM. EWM stays the transactional and execution backbone. An orchestration layer on SAP BTP / SAP Integration Suite can bring together SAP EWM, SAP TM/Yard, RTLS, IoT/equipment telemetry, external carrier events, mobile devices, and warehouse automation. The layer evaluates that live context and determines the next best action, while EWM and defined business rules stay the execution and governance foundation.

Today, many warehouses effectively run: WMS → Task → Worker → Confirmation.

The model above runs as a loop instead: Warehouse State → Agent → Next Best Move → Execution → New Warehouse State → Agent. A truck delay doesn't just trigger an alert - it can shift priorities. A forklift finishing putaway doesn't just close a task - it triggers a new optimization decision. A replenishment isn't just sitting in a queue - its downstream impact on blocked picks becomes part of the decision itself.

Two Questions I'd Push Back On Myself

How much autonomy should this have? Not full autonomy, at least not on day one. A tiered model makes more sense - consistent with how SAP has generally framed agent autonomy in its 2026 releases: the agent can suggest, execute with notification, or escalate, depending on the risk and reversibility of the action. Cross-zone reassignments go to a supervisor. Low-risk, in-area re-sequencing can auto-execute with a logged, visible trail. Anything touching safety or labor agreements escalates by default. Warehouse operations involve people and equipment - autonomy should be earned over time, not assumed from the start.

What has to be true before any of this works? Clean master data, standardized system-driven processes, and reliable real-time location/equipment feeds. An orchestration layer is only as good as the data feeding it - a heavily customized, inconsistent EWM landscape will produce unreliable recommendations no matter how good the decision logic is. Warehouses that fix this foundation first will be positioned to adopt next-best-move capabilities - whether custom-built on BTP or adopted through SAP's own EWM Real-Time Optimization Agent as it matures - much faster than those that treat AI readiness as a separate, later project.

Bringing It Together

SAP EWM already provides the foundation. The shift is in the guiding question - from “which task should I assign?” to “what is the best physical move for this warehouse right now?”

  • EWM provides transactional truth.
  • Real-time systems (RTLS, IoT, telemetry) provide physical truth.
  • AI provides decision intelligence.
  • SAP BTP provides orchestration.
  • Automation and RF provide execution.

The future of warehouse execution probably isn't about pushing more tasks through the system faster. It's about making better decisions between every task - continuously, and with enough governance and data discipline to trust those decisions.

The next task is easy to find. The next best move is the real warehouse execution challenge.

I'd be curious how others are seeing this play out - has anyone started piloting real-time re-sequencing on top of EWM's existing interleaving logic, either through SAP's own roadmap capabilities or a custom BTP extension? Drop a comment below.

entry.title: Why Human Oversight Matters More Than Ever and What It Means
entry.content:
Deploying AI agents in an organization: Is it fun if it isn’t safe?

With the advent of AI agents, there is increasing interest in a topic that had been around for a long time in the AI Ethics world: Human oversight and determination. But why did it become so important now, and what does it mean?

Unlike generative AI that waits for our prompts and then generates output, AI agents are different creatures entirely. They plan, reflect, use tools, collaborate with other agents, remember, and most importantly, they can act autonomously.

This shift from stateless, single-step outputs to stateful, multi-step, goal-directed systems introduces new safety risks, often referred to as cascading effects: Through reasoning and execution chains, agents take one step’s output as the next step’s input which can turn one isolated error into a cross-system trajectory.

Imagine a company that deploys an AI agent to manage vendor onboarding: Because the input data is incomplete or ambiguous, the agent incorrectly classifies a vendor as “low risk”. It then skips enhanced due diligence, approves the vendor, creates the vendor record in the ERP system, generates a contract template, and enables payment processing. Later audits rely on these records, making the original mistake harder to detect. What began as a single misclassification becomes a chain of errors across interconnected systems.

With generative AI, the worst-case outcome may be a hallucinated response to a prompt. With AI agents, however, we delegate decisions and actions to agentic systems which introduces additional safety concerns and amplifies risks. In many cases, meaningful human oversight can minimize these risks. But autonomy and oversight are in constant tension: the more the system decides on its own, the harder it becomes to keep humans genuinely in control.

In this blog post series, we will therefore answer the question: How do we keep humans meaningfully involved as AI systems get more autonomous every day?

From Risk to Harm: Understanding What's Actually at Stake

Let's get clear on terminology, because it matters. Risk is the possibility of something going wrong. Harm is what happens when it does.

Consider these scenarios:

Example

Risk

Harm

A personal AI agent is given authority to manage a user’s calendar and email inbox, and it independently sends a meeting cancellation to the wrong recipients.

The agent misinterprets the user’s intent and propagates an error across multiple tools.

Confidential information is disclosed and professional relationships are damaged.

An AI procurement agent is allowed to purchase goods on behalf of a user, and it completes a transaction that exceeds budget, policy, or necessity.

The agent optimizes the wrong objective, fails to respect constraints, or cannot reliably distinguish a tentative instruction from an authorization to act.

Companies cope with financial losses, compliance violations, and auditability issues.

An AI recruitment agent automatically shortlists candidates for a given job posting, but it repeatedly deprioritizes certain applicants.

The agent reinforces historical bias across multiple screening steps or cannot justify why one candidate is favored over another.

Qualified candidates are rejected, resulting in unexplained exclusion and the reinforcement of workplace discrimination.

Here's something that complicates matters further: An AI agent that's ethically compliant in one context might be completely inappropriate in another. Fairness in a criminal justice system looks nothing like fairness in healthcare allocation.

To mitigate risks and avoid harm, humans must be adequately involved in AI decision-making, with transparency, auditability, and the authority to intervene when needed, understand what went wrong when things fail, and ensure that no machine ever makes high-stakes decisions without meaningful human accountability. “Adequately” means that human oversight is not a one-size-fits-all solution but must be implemented with context-sensitive controls that weigh the benefits of automation with its risks and possible harms. This does not only apply to AI agents but to applications leveraging traditional ML models and Generative AI too. What changes with agents is the urgency and the consequence of getting it wrong.

Three Layers of Human Oversight for AI Systems

Now, how does human oversight look like? In the SAP Global AI Ethics Policy, based on the Ethics Guidelines by the EU High-Level Expert Group on AI, human oversight and determination are defined as “Human monitors, evaluates, and/or validates AI Systems’ output and, if needed, intervenes. Different mechanisms of Human Oversight include Human-in-command, Human-in-the-loop, and Human-on-the-loop, among others.”

When an AI system only makes suggestions – producing recommendations, scores, or summaries that a human then acts upon – this is called AI assistance. The system is not engineered with formal checkpoints; the focus is on augmentation, not so much on automation. Human oversight mechanisms are largely not necessary since no authority or control has been delegated; the human retains full decision authority by design.

The oversight question becomes meaningful when systems begin to act, namely when they execute, transact, modify, or trigger downstream processes on their own. Three distinct but not mutually exclusive modes of oversight apply to that space:

1. Human-in-the-Loop: The Checkpoint

Human-in-the-loop (HITL) introduces defined control points in the decision pipeline where human approval or validation is necessary, particularly when (erroneous) actions carry elevated risk or irreversible consequences. SAP’s Global AI Ethics Policy defines HITL as “human involvement in every decision of the AI System, such as validating or correcting output”.

The key is knowing when to require human approval (not for everything) and ensuring approvers have the full context they need to make an informed decision. “Informed decisions” depend on transparency and explainability. A human cannot meaningfully approve or reject what they cannot understand. If the AI’s reasoning, inputs, and confidence are opaque, HITL collapses into blind approval, regardless of how carefully the checkpoint is designed.

While AI assistance usually describes a mode where the AI plays a supportive, non-deciding role for a human operator, HITL is a specific system design pattern that requires human decision-making at critical points for accountability and shared control. The line between AI assistance and HITL can be fuzzy in practice. The distinction often comes down to how much of the follow-up action is automated once the human has decided.

2. Human-on-the-Loop: The Supervisor

AI systems, especially AI agents, can fully automate processes and even operate autonomously, but they need human supervision. SAP’s Global AI Ethics Policy defines human-on-the-loop (HOTL) as “Human monitors the AI System’s operation and intervenes, if necessary.” This isn't about approving every action, it's about stepping in if things go wrong, monitoring behavioral patterns, being alert for vulnerabilities, and creating continuous feedback loops.

The level of monitoring must match the risk: A sandbox experiment with synthetic data doesn't need the same scrutiny as an AI making hiring decisions or controlling industrial systems. While high-risk systems will require daily or weekly oversight via dashboards, regular deep dives into decision logic and patterns, and the ability to interrupt the system at any point during its operation, low-risk AI systems might be sufficiently governable with monthly or quarterly reviews.

3. Human-in-Command: The Safety Net

Human-in-command (HIC) is a governance principle and constitutes the baseline for human control over AI systems. SAP’s Global AI Ethics Policy describes HIC as the ability to oversee an AI system’s overall activity, including its wider economic, societal, legal, and ethical impacts, and to decide when and how the system should be used. This includes choosing not to use an AI system in a specific context, setting levels of human discretion during use, or ensuring that humans can override system decisions.

Even when an AI system does not pose significant ethical risk or potential harm, humans must retain ultimate authority. At SAP, this means avoiding something like a “human-out-of-the-loop” model where AI completes its mission without the possibility of humans to intervene, or when AI can change its intended domain of use or goals without human control.

How SAP Classifies AI According to Ethical Risks

This might be a good time to introduce SAP’s AI Ethics Assessment process, because it helps determining the criticality of human oversight and preparing its implementation. AI use cases are classified into three SAP-internal risk categories: Prohibited, high-risk, and standard. While there is more to learn about the process and categories in SAP’s AI Ethics Handbook, it is important to understand that for high-risk AI like HR use cases, a human-in-the-loop is usually required. Why? Because a wrong decision could lead to serious personal harm, and we want to mitigate that risk as much as possible.

HOTL measures are to be incorporated by all use cases, although the implementation may vary according to the specific risks. And HIC is SAP’s baseline principle that equally applies to all use cases regardless of their internal risk classification.

What to Expect from this Blog Post Series

That covers the theory, but real-world implementations are often less clear-cut. Over the next four posts, we’ll examine several SAP AI use cases and see which human oversight mechanisms they reflect. We’ll look at a use case that illustrates what HITL oversight looks like in practice, and how it can fail. We’ll then ask a harder question: is having a human in the loop enough to guarantee meaningful oversight? Next, we’ll turn to a HOTL use case that shifts responsibilities between humans and AI over time. And finally, we’ll zoom out to the ecosystem level and ask what human oversight can look like when hundreds of agents operate at once in an Autonomous Enterprise.

A Note on Transparency. Speaking of ethics principles, transparency is another one we take seriously. So, in the spirit of practicing what we preach: GenAI assisted in the creation of this blog post series. Its job? Giving feedback on structure, tone, and making suggestions for clarity and conciseness across multiple iterations. The image on top of the blog post was also modified by AI. The ideas, the arguments, and the accountability remain thoroughly human.

Read More

Next in this series:

  • More than a Checkpoint: Human-in-the-loop in Practice
  • Trust Isn't Enough: Validating Human-in-the-Loop for Oversight
  • From AI Assistance to Human-on-the-Loop: A Compliance Detection Case Study
  • When Agents Multiply: Human Oversight in the Autonomous Enterprise

SAP resources:

  • Responsible AI at SAP
  • SAP Global AI Ethics Policy
  • SAP AI Ethics Handbook
  • Autonomous Enterprise

External resources:

  • European Commission, 2019, Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI by EU High-Level Expert Group on AI

entry.title: From Alerts to Autonomous Action: Building AI Agents for EWM Exception Handling with Joule
entry.content:
If you've spent any time in the Warehouse Monitor, you know the drill: a wave of alerts fires, a warehouse task fails, a bin comes up empty during putaway, and a key user goes hunting through node after node to figure out what broke and why. It works - but it's reactive, manual, and it doesn't scale as warehouses get busier and leaner on staff.

At the same time, SAP has been telegraphing a shift toward agentic AI across its logistics portfolio - Joule agents, "AI for Logistics," and sessions like Managing Warehouse Incidents with AI Agents at LogiMAT 2026. The vision is compelling: instead of a human triaging every exception, an agent monitors, reasons, and acts - closing the loop without a person in the middle for the routine cases.

What's missing from the conversation so far is the practical, EWM-specific version of this story: which exceptions are actually good candidates for agentic handling, what would the architecture look like, and where do you draw the guardrails? That's what this post digs into.

Start with the exceptions you already know

Before talking about agents, it helps to inventory what "exception handling" looks like in EWM today. A few familiar examples:

  • No empty bin found during automatic putaway (common after a Usage Decision/quality posting change or a bin-to-bin transfer).
  • Warehouse Task (WT) failures due to blocked resources, HU inconsistencies, or storage type capacity checks.
  • Wave/Resource imbalance - one activity area is drowning in open tasks while another sits idle.
  • RF confirmation errors - quantity mismatches, missing HUs, or expired batches surfacing mid-pick.

Today, each of these routes to a human: a key user checks the Warehouse Monitor, applies judgment, and manually triggers a fix (reassign a bin, cancel and recreate a WT, rebalance a resource group). It's exactly the kind of "detect → decide → act" loop that agentic AI is built for - provided the decision space is bounded and the action is reversible or low-risk.

What an agent actually adds

An AI agent isn't magic - it's a loop of three capabilities layered on top of what already exists in EWM:

  1. Perception - reading Warehouse Monitor alerts, exception codes, and queue/resource status in near-real time (via APIs rather than a human staring at a screen).
  2. Reasoning - using a model (Joule, or a custom LLM-backed service) to interpret the exception in context: is this a one-off, or the third "no empty bin" alert in this storage type this hour?
  3. Action - calling back into EWM (via released APIs / RFC-enabled function modules / OData services) to execute a bounded corrective action: reassign a destination bin, trigger a replenishment WT, or escalate to a human if confidence is low.

The key architectural point: the agent doesn't replace EWM's process logic - it sits alongside it as an orchestration layer, watching outputs and calling the same interfaces a key user or an RF device would use.

A worked example

Take the classic "no empty bin found after UD" scenario from quality inspection stock release:

  • Today: the WT fails, an alert appears in the Monitor, a key user investigates, checks storage type capacity, manually assigns an alternate bin, and re-releases the task.
  • With an agent: the event fires into the agent, which checks (a) is there genuinely no capacity, or a data/master-data issue, (b) are there eligible bins in an adjacent storage section that meet putaway strategy rules, and (c) has this happened repeatedly for this material/storage type combination (a signal for a slotting problem, not a one-off). Based on that, it either auto-assigns a valid alternate bin and re-triggers the WT, or escalates with a recommendation ("storage type 0020 is at 94% capacity - consider a slotting review") rather than just raising a raw error.

Notice what changed: the system logic for finding a valid bin hasn't moved - EWM still owns that. What the agent adds is the judgment call of when to act automatically vs. flag for a human, plus a bit of pattern recognition across repeated exceptions that a person triaging one alert at a time would likely miss.

Where the guardrails need to be

This is the part that tends to get glossed over in vendor demos, so it's worth being explicit:

  • Bound the action space. An agent should only be allowed to trigger actions from a pre-approved, low-risk set (bin reassignment within existing storage-type rules, resource rebalancing, WT recreation) - not master data changes or anything touching financial postings.
  • Confidence thresholds and human-in-the-loop fallback. If the agent isn't confident, the default should be escalate, not guess. This is a warehouse floor, not a chatbot - a wrong autonomous action has physical, inventory-accuracy consequences.
  • Full audit trail. Every agent-triggered action should be logged with the same rigor as a manual change (who/what triggered it, based on what reasoning), both for compliance and for tuning the agent over time.
  • Start narrow. Pick one or two exception types with clear, well-understood resolution logic (bin reassignment is a great first candidate) before expanding scope. Resist the urge to let an agent "handle exceptions" broadly on day one.

The takeaway

Agentic AI in EWM isn't about replacing the Warehouse Monitor or the key user - it's about narrowing the gap between "alert fired" and "problem fixed" for the well-understood, repetitive exceptions that currently eat up key-user time. The technology to start experimenting with this exists today in the SAP ecosystem (Joule, BTP, EWM's existing APIs); what's been missing is a clear-eyed, practitioner-level conversation about how to apply it responsibly. Hopefully this is a useful starting point for that conversation.

Have you experimented with agent-based automation around EWM exceptions - even informally, with scripts or bots? I'd love to hear what's worked (and what hasn't) in the comments.

entry.title: Why Clean Core Became an AI Precondition (Series 3, Part 1: Clean Core + AI)
entry.content:
Why Clean Core Became an AI Precondition

By Deepa Dorairaj | SAP AI Solution Architect | Series 3, Part 1 of 6 | Published September 2026

TL;DR: Clean Core used to be sold as an upgrade-hygiene practice — keep your core standard, extensions modular, upgrades painless. That framing undersold it. In 2026, clean core became something closer to a precondition: enterprises signing RISE with SAP deals this year — Airbus, Shell, Morgan Stanley, Eli Lilly among them — aren't just modernizing their ERP. They're building the only kind of landscape an AI agent can actually reason over reliably. This article makes the case for why, and sets up the rest of this series: how to assess your own clean core state, what SAP's own agents do about it, and how to avoid the most common failure mode — moving technical debt instead of removing it.

Series Context

This opens Series 3, following the six-part Agentic AI in Practice series earlier this year. That series built agents from the ground up — ReAct patterns, multi-agent orchestration, migration assessment, human-in-the-loop design, production systems. This series asks a different question: what does the landscape underneath those agents need to look like for any of that to actually hold up in production? Clean Core is the answer, and this series treats it as an engineering discipline, not a compliance checkbox.

SECTION 1 — THE PATTERN: WHY FIVE MAJOR ENTERPRISES SIGNED RISE THE SAME QUARTER

In Q2 2026, SAP closed RISE with SAP deals with Airbus, Shell, Morgan Stanley, Eli Lilly, Samsonite, and Vonovia. Different industries, different geographies, different starting landscapes. The one thing they share: each deal is explicitly built around a Clean Core foundation, not just a cloud migration.

Airbus's deal is the clearest example. It's a RISE with SAP engagement for 100,000+ employees, paired with sovereign cloud infrastructure, explicitly framed around building "a clean core, simplified processes, and a scalable architecture" as the foundation for AI agents and intelligent automation across manufacturing, supply chain, finance, and customer service.

That clustering isn't a coincidence of sales timing. It's a signal that a specific class of enterprise — the kind with decades of accumulated customization — has independently concluded the same thing: you can't bolt agentic AI onto a landscape the way you bolted on a new report or a custom workflow. The AI needs the landscape itself to change first.

SECTION 2 — WHY AGENTS NEED WHAT CUSTOM CODE BREAKS

Here's the mechanical reason, stated plainly: an AI agent reasoning over your SAP landscape needs predictable APIs and consistent data models. It needs to know that a "customer" object behaves the same way in every business unit, that a given API is stable and documented, that a process follows the same logic across the enterprise rather than a different Z-program's version of that logic in every plant or region.

A landscape full of one-off Z-programs, undocumented BAdI implementations, and modifications layered over twenty years doesn't give an agent that consistency. It gives the agent a maze — and worse, a maze where the walls move depending on which company code you're in. An agent can't reliably automate a process it can't consistently model. When it hits a Z-program with undocumented business logic, it either breaks silently, produces a wrong answer with false confidence, or needs a human to hand-hold it through the edge case — which defeats the entire point of deploying it.

This is why "AI readiness" and "clean core readiness" have effectively become the same conversation. SAP's own Custom Code Migration Agent — covered later in this series — makes this literal: before an agent can be trusted with an S/4HANA readiness assessment, someone (or something) has to first assess how much custom code stands between the current landscape and the standardized one an agent can actually reason over.

SECTION 3 — THE PART MOST ROADMAPS UNDERSELL: WHAT "CLEAN" ACTUALLY COSTS

Clean Core done right increases long-term agility. Clean Core done under deadline pressure just relocates technical debt from ABAP into the BTP extension layer with a nicer name — the same one-off business logic, now living in CAPM instead of a Z-program, still undocumented, still fragile, just wearing a more modern architecture.

This is the failure mode worth naming honestly, because most vendor material won't: migrating a Z-program's logic 1:1 into a CAP service isn't clean core. It's a translation exercise. Real clean core work means asking, for every piece of custom logic, whether it encodes a genuine competitive differentiator or just an inherited decision nobody has re-justified since it was written. That decision-cost — not the technical lift of moving code — is what actually eats a migration's calendar. The technical work is estimable. The re-justification isn't.

SECTION 4 — WHERE THIS SERIES GOES FROM HERE

The rest of this series treats clean core as something you can actually assess, execute, and govern — not just aspire to:

  • Part 2 covers how to assess clean core readiness without RISE — ABAP Test Cockpit's clean core checks, the Cloudification Repository, Project Kernseife for scoring technical debt, and the Clean Core Levels A–D framework for prioritizing what to fix first.
  • Part 3 goes inside SAP's S/4HANA Custom Code Migration Agent — how an agentic loop actually runs ATC checks, applies deterministic quick fixes, and where human judgment still has to sit.
  • Part 4 addresses the relocation problem directly — concrete governance patterns for side-by-side extensibility that avoid just moving debt into BTP.
  • Part 5 applies SAP's own "three concentric circles" model (ABAP Cloud, ABAP AI, agents) to a real worked example.
  • Part 6 closes the series by tying clean core to agent governance infrastructure — MCP Gateway, AI Agent Hub verification — showing how a clean core is what makes agent governance enforceable rather than aspirational.

The throughline across all six parts: clean core isn't a 2026 trend that fades once the next architecture pattern arrives. It's the infrastructure discipline every future wave of enterprise AI — agents today, whatever comes after agents — will keep depending on.

entry.title: More than a Checkpoint: Human-in-the-loop in Practice
entry.content:
How can we define mandatory control points in the AI agent’s decision-making chain?

What does it actually mean for a human to be "in the loop"? 

In our first blog post of this series, we introduced the concept of human oversight in AI systems and explored the spectrum of human–AI collaboration from AI assistance to full autonomy. 

Today, we make things concrete. We look at one real SAP use case that illustrates what human-in-the-loop (HITL) oversight looks like in practice: a Dispute Resolution Agent. 

The Dispute Resolution Agent 

What It Does 

The Dispute Resolution Agent supports contract accountants working on dispute cases: think incorrect invoices, missing payments, or billing discrepancies. For each incoming case, the agent automatically: 

  • Analyzes invoice details, payment histories, and contract terms, 
  • summarizes the key issues, and proposes a set of resolution options to the contract accountant. 

The human accountant then reviews the agent's analysis, inspects the reasoning and supporting documents behind each proposed option, and selects one. From that point, execution is back with the agent – the accountant's role is the decision, not the follow-through. 

Figure 1: The Dispute Resolution Agent presents a concise summary of a dispute case as well as possible resolution options to the human accountant for review and selection.

Figure 2: The AI Analysis view shows the agent's reasoning, the actions it took, other engaged agents, and the data sources accessed.

What Makes this Use Case an Example of HITL Implementation? 

It is worth being precise about what kind of oversight is happening here. Why is this a good example of the human-in-the-loop paradigm? 

The agent operates with substantial autonomy: It analyzes cases, synthesizes evidence across multiple data sources, and generates resolution proposals without being prompted step by step. The heavy lifting is done by the AI. This goes well beyond AI assistance. 

But the oversight design goes beyond human-on-the-loop (HOTL) principles too. The workflow does not allow the agent to act automatically while humans monitor and correct after the work is already done. The loop is interrupted for every case, and the accountant must select a resolution before anything is executed. Human approval is mandatory, not conditional. 

This mandatory human decision point for every consequential action is what characterizes HITL oversight. The agent cannot reach an outcome without explicit human approval. That approval is an informed decision: the agent shares its full analysis and reasoning alongside the proposed options. 

Why the Stakes Demand Human Review 

Consider what the risk landscape would look like if proposed resolutions were applied automatically: 

Broad access scope. The agent requires access to invoice records, payment histories, contract terms, and communication threads. Broad access scopes combined with autonomous execution create meaningful risk exposure. Unintended actions – such as applying credits that were not earned – can reach further than expected. 

Multi-agent collaboration. The stakes increase further when the Dispute Resolution Agent operates alongside other specialized agents covering areas such as financial accounting and cash collection. A resolution that looks correct at the dispute stage can silently trigger a chain of downstream actions: an entry removing an outstanding balance from the books, a payment release updating a customer's credit status. Each downstream agent acts on what it receives, with no way to detect that something went wrong upstream.  

Responsibility gaps. A resolution executed without human review cannot be traced back to a deliberate human judgment. If something goes wrong, accountability becomes unclear – neither the accountant nor the organization made a conscious choice. 

Goal drift.  AI systems can change over time. An agent might gradually favor faster case closure over accurate resolution. Without a human reviewing outcomes, this drift could go undetected until the consequences show up in customer complaints. 

These risks, if unaddressed, could lead to real-world harm: Dispute resolution involves financial decisions that directly affect customers and company revenue. An incorrectly resolved dispute – whether in favor of or against the customer – can have immediate financial consequences, damage relationships, and in some cases carry legal implications. The impact of errors is high. 

Human review and approval before execution address all four risks. They keep accountability with the accountant, create a natural checkpoint for detecting drift, ensure that broad access to multiple systems is mediated by a human, and mitigate the risk of downstream error propagation. The human approval step is therefore not only a check on one decision – it actively avoids real-world harm. 

The Challenges HITL Does Not Automatically Solve 

Requiring human approval is not the same as ensuring meaningful human oversight. Three well-documented failure modes are worth understanding, and each has specific implications for the dispute resolution use case. 

Automation Bias 

Automation bias is the tendency to over-rely on automated suggestions, treating them as correct by default rather than as inputs that require evaluation. It has been observed in pilots, healthcare professionals, and software developers alike [see 1-3].

In the dispute resolution context, automation bias would look like an accountant who consistently selects the agent's top recommendation without working through the underlying analysis – blindly trusting the agent's judgment rather than exercising their own. This effect may only build over time: once the agent has been performing reliably, it becomes increasingly difficult to justify the effort of scrutinizing each recommendation. The line between reasonable trust and over-reliance is easy to cross without noticing. 

One way to push back against this is to build transparency directly into the workflow: when the agent's reasoning is clearly stated, engaging with it becomes the path of least resistance. Figure 2 shows how the dispute resolution agent puts this into practice: beyond general case information, accountants can inspect the agent's chain of thought, the steps it executed, which other agents were involved, and exactly which data sources were accessed. 

Decision Fatigue

Decision fatigue is the deterioration of decision quality after a sustained sequence of decisions. The more choices a person makes, the harder it becomes to evaluate each subsequent one carefully [see 4].

An accountant processing a high volume of dispute cases in a single sitting is exposed to this risk: the work becomes monotonous. When case after case presents the same patterns, the mind stops treating each one as a new problem. Attention narrows, nuance gets missed, and genuinely anomalous cases can slip through undetected simply because they arrive after the tenth routine one. Careful evaluation is cognitively expensive, and that resource depletes. 

Structuring workloads so that accountants handle a bounded set of cases in a session, rather than an open-ended queue, reduces this exposure. The dispute resolution agent supports this by prioritizing incoming cases – so that when attention is freshest, it is directed at the cases that matter most.  

Cognitive Overload

Cognitive overload occurs when the volume or complexity of information presented to a reviewer exceeds their processing capacity. It is related to, but distinct from, decision fatigue: fatigue is about quantity over time, overload is about complexity in the moment [see 5, 6].

For the Dispute Resolution Agent, each case involves invoice records, payment histories, contract terms, agent-performed actions, and resolution options – all potentially relevant to the decision. If this information is not structured carefully, the cognitive demand of a single case can exceed what a reviewer can meaningfully process. 

Part of the answer is in how the output is presented: rather than overwhelming the accountant with everything at once, the interface shows only what is relevant to the case at hand. Figure 2 illustrates this directly for the dispute resolution agent. Information is grouped under clear headers – Actions, Summary, Data Sources, Engaged Agents – so the accountant can orient quickly. Details that would clutter the overview, such as the full text of supporting documents, are accessible through links rather than surfaced by default. 

But careful interface design only takes you so far. It works for its intended purpose only if the reviewer has the domain expertise to interrogate what the agent produces. A structured output handed to someone unfamiliar with dispute resolution does not lead to meaningful oversight. In this example, an accountant brings real knowledge of contracts, billing, and what a fair resolution looks like. 

What This Use Case Teaches Us 

The Dispute Resolution Agent illustrates what it means to implement HITL with care: the agent handles the analysis, the human retains the decision, and the design ensures that decision can be made on informed grounds. 

But the failure modes discussed above – automation bias, decision fatigue, cognitive overload – are not theoretical. They are genuine oversight challenges. Building a HITL checkpoint into a workflow is the beginning of human oversight, not the end. What makes it meaningful is the combination of transparency, workload design, and interface structure that supports the human in exercising judgment. 

Want to dive deeper? Our next post in this series asks whether trust in human oversight is itself enough to ensure that it is meaningful – and what it actually takes to validate the performance of the human in the loop.

A Note on Transparency. Speaking of ethics principles, transparency is another one we take seriously. So, in the spirit of practicing what we preach: GenAI assisted in the creation of this blog post series. Its job? Giving feedback on structure, tone, and making suggestions for clarity and conciseness across multiple iterations. The image on top of the blog post was also modified by AI. The ideas, the arguments, and the accountability remain thoroughly human.

Further Reading

Next in this series: 

  • Trust Isn't Enough: Validating Human-in-the-Loop for Oversight

  • When Agents Multiply: Human Oversight in the Autonomous Enterprise

[2] Mosier, K. L., & Manzey, D. (2019). Humans and automated decision aids: A match made in heaven? https://depositonce.tu-berlin.de/items/b2e2d621-a3af-4daa-bf19-b4bf4f5bd8eb

[5] Bedard, J., Kropp, M., Hsu, M., Karaman, O. T., Hawes, J., & Kellerman, G. R. (2026). When Using AI Leads to “Brain Fry.” https://hbr.org/2026/03/when-using-ai-leads-to-brain-fry   

[6] Shalu, Verma, N., Dev, K., Bhardwaj, A. B., & Kumar, K. (2025) The Cognitive Cost of AI: How AI Anxiety and Attitudes Influence Decision Fatigue in Daily Technology Use. Annals of Neurosciences, 33(1), 73–84: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12367725/

entry.title: The Missing Layer in Autonomous Warehousing: Warehouse Decision Memory
entry.content:
The Missing Layer in Autonomous Warehousing: Warehouse Decision Memory

 
Introduction
 
Warehouse Management systems are very good at recording what happened in the warehouse. But there is another layer of knowledge that is often missing — the reasoning behind the decisions experienced warehouse supervisors make every day. In this blog, I explore the concept of Warehouse Decision Memory and how SAP EWM, together with AI and SAP BTP, could capture these decisions, their context and outcomes to gradually build more intelligent warehouse execution.
 

I keep seeing the same thing in warehouse operations: the best supervisors often make decisions that the system did not recommend.

Your best supervisor makes a decision that isn't exactly what the system recommended. Maybe they change a task priority, move an operator to a different zone, or trigger replenishment earlier than planned. Most of the time, there's a good reason behind it.

I have seen this happen in real operations discussions: the system looks correct on paper, but the supervisor has a dock constraint, a delayed truck, or a customer escalation in mind that the standard strategy simply does not know at that moment.

The problem is that EWM records what happened, but not really why the decision was made. That knowledge stays with the person - and when they move to another site, change roles, or leave the organization, a lot of that experience leaves with them.

What if we could capture that knowledge?

This is where I feel AI in EWM can help in a practical way. I would call it Warehouse Decision Memory. The idea is simple:

System Recommendation → Warehouse Context → Human Decision → Outcome → Learning

For example, EWM recommends this sequence:

Putaway → Replenishment → Picking

But the supervisor changes it to:

Replenishment → Picking → Putaway

Why? It could be any of these:

  • A priority truck is leaving soon
  • Stock for an important order is running low
  • A specific operator happens to be available in that zone
  • There's congestion building up elsewhere
  • The goods carry a higher business priority
  • The supervisor just knows something the standard rules don't see

Today, that reasoning usually isn't captured anywhere in a structured way. That's the part worth fixing.

It is not only about adding one more KPI

Warehouses already run with many KPIs - distance, labor utilization, task age, throughput, resource availability. All of them matter. But in my experience, good supervisors do not decide based on one number alone. They look at what is happening on the floor and then take a call.

That is the part AI agents will eventually need to understand. Not just:

"Which task is closest?"

But:

"Given the current warehouse situation, which decision creates the highest operational value?"

And that answer can change from one minute to the next.

How I would start thinking about this

I do not think we need to rebuild EWM for this. EWM already has a lot of the operational picture. What is missing is the reason why a person moves away from the system recommendation, and what was happening in the warehouse at that time:

  • Open outbound demand
  • Delivery priority
  • Resource availability
  • Exception backlog
  • Inventory situation
  • Truck and dock constraints
  • Travel distance
  • Time of day

Then capture the outcome that followed: Did the order ship on time? Was an SLA breach avoided? Did the decision create rework, or reduce congestion?

Over time, patterns start to emerge.

This is the part I find interesting

Think of a situation where an AI agent looks at the current warehouse condition and says:

"The standard strategy recommends putaway first. However, in 78 similar situations, supervisors prioritized replenishment when outbound demand was within 60 minutes - and those decisions were associated with better on-time shipment performance."

To me, that is much more useful than a static rule saying "replenishment has higher priority." The agent is not just following a rule. It is learning from similar situations, the context around them, and the outcome that followed - while the supervisor still has the final say.

One thing we should be careful about

We can't assume every good outcome was caused by the decision that preceded it. Warehouse operations are complex - a truck leaving on time may have nothing to do with one particular override.

So for me, the hard part is not only collecting more data. It is understanding whether that decision actually changed the outcome. Otherwise, we may just end up training a model on past transactions and confusing correlation with real learning.

Where I would begin

I would not try to capture every decision in the warehouse from day one. I would pick one clear use case - for example, manual task-priority overrides during peak operations - and capture:

Recommendation → Context → Decision → Outcome

Run it for one peak season and see what the data tells you.

If we can identify real patterns in how experienced supervisors make these calls, that would be valuable. We would not just be automating warehouse processes. We would be starting to retain some of the warehouse experience that usually stays in people's heads. For me, that is one of the missing pieces on the road to autonomous warehouse execution. The future warehouse should not only know what happened. It should slowly learn why experienced people chose to do something differently.

That is why I feel Warehouse Decision Memory is worth exploring.

Conclusion

The journey towards autonomous warehouse execution is not only about giving AI access to more data or automating more tasks. It is also about capturing the experience and decision-making that already exists on the warehouse floor. Warehouse Decision Memory could provide a way to turn those human decisions into reusable knowledge, helping future AI agents make more context-aware and explainable decisions while keeping humans in the loop.

Would love to hear from the EWM and warehouse community: are you already capturing the reasoning behind manual overrides, or only the final transaction? That might be the first real step toward a warehouse that learns.

entry.title: Trust Isn't Enough: Validating Human-in-the-Loop for Oversight
entry.content:
How can we prevent the human-in-the-loop from becoming the dummy-in-the-loop?

When we deploy an AI model, we measure everything. From accuracy, precision, recall, confidence scores to benchmark performance. Having these numbers gives us the confidence that our system is performing as expected. 

To oversee its output, we also add a human to the system. But when we do that, we treat the human as a well-working tool for oversight, not as another variable. We simply trust that a human in the loop is enough to establish true oversight.  

But is trust enough? Are humans a validated control just because they are present? 

Why the Human is in the Loop in the First Place 

Human-in-the-loop (HITL) means that before an AI system’s recommendation becomes an action, a human reviews and approves or rejects it. The idea is straightforward: a human in the loop can catch errors, apply judgment, and remain accountable in ways that a model alone cannot. 

This has become a central part of how organizations govern AI. The EU AI Act requires human oversight for high-risk AI systems. Companies use HITL as a compliance argument and a way to build trust with customers who often prioritize staying in control of (agentic) AI systems.  

At SAP, HITL is one of the core controls in our approach to trustworthy AI. So, how can we be sure that HITL remains effective and not just present? 

Degraded Oversight in Practice 

Consider what degraded oversight looks like in practice and why it is so hard to detect. 

Imagine an AI agent is deployed in a security operations center. It analyzes incoming alerts and proposes actions (dismiss alert, escalate, block this account). Analysts review and approve or reject each one. 

In the first weeks, analysts are careful. They ask follow-up questions, push back when necessary, and occasionally override the AI decisions. Three months later, the same analysts are handling twice the volume of incoming alerts. The model has been reliable for weeks. Reviews that used to take two minutes now take twenty seconds. The acceptance rate has climbed steadily. 

Is this a sign that the system has improved? Perhaps. The model may have improved, and analysts may have learned when to trust it. But it could also mean something entirely different: oversight has quietly degraded. Analysts may no longer be critically evaluating recommendations; they may simply be approving them. 

From the outside, these two situations can look almost identical. Fast review times and high acceptance rates could indicate an excellent AI system, or they could signal that human reviews are no longer carried out thoroughly. 

Why Oversight Degrades 

A scenario like this may be exaggerated, but it is not a fictional edge case. Research has already documented three mechanisms that affect HITL effectiveness: 

  • Automation bias is the tendency to over-trust an automated system and stop critically evaluating its outputs.  
  • Decision fatigue is the decline in decision quality under prolonged or repetitive tasks. 
  • Cognitive Overload happens when the volume or complexity of decisions exceeds the capacity the reviewer can process. 

These mechanisms often develop gradually rather than suddenly. What makes them particularly problematic is that they can remain invisible to the metrics organizations typically monitor. 

The Blind Spot in Today’s Evaluations 

In human-AI-collaboration, most measurements still focus on the AI system itself. We ask whether model accuracy improved, whether explanations increase user trust or acceptance rate. If the human reviewer is studied, the evaluation typically happens after a session is done. Retroactive questionnaires that assess workload, trust, and user satisfaction are useful for understanding trends, but they cannot catch and prevent problems while they are developing. In the example scenario a security reviewer experiencing all three mechanisms can still show a high approval rate, fast review times, and report reasonable satisfaction in a post-session survey. By the time a pattern shows up, many decisions may have already been made and the gaps in oversight had real consequences.  

In other words, we have extensive monitoring for model performance but almost none for the quality of the human oversight that governs it. 

How Agentic AI Raises the Stakes

This gap becomes significantly more important as AI systems become increasingly agentic. 

Early AI tools handled tasks with limited scopes: classifying an image, recommending a product, or processing an invoice. Nowadays, agentic AI systems execute multi-step workflows, make sequences of decisions, and act with increasing autonomy over extended periods. The volume of decisions human reviewers must oversee increases. Similarly, the context needed for a single decision gets more complex and consequences become difficult to trace across long sequences of actions. 

What Measurements Can Help? 

To be direct: There is currently no established, validated framework for monitoring HITL effectiveness in real time. This is a gap in both research and practice.  

One starting point could be the monitoring of behavioral signals. In a software-based review workflow, how long someone takes to act on a recommendation is easily observable. Both extremes may hint at underlying problems: very fast decisions may indicate rubber-stamping; very slow ones may indicate confusion or overload.

Other signals worth tracking could include how often reviewers override or correct outputs, how deeply they engage with the underlying content, and whether their decisions are consistent across similar cases. 

None of these are reliable signals on their own. Fast reviewers are not necessarily disengaged. High acceptance rates may reflect a good model, not an overworked analyst. The challenge is detecting and interpreting patterns over time, in context. This is harder than it sounds and is yet to be systematically studied.

A more direct approach could be the introduction of controlled test outputs, i.e. deliberately injecting known-incorrect AI recommendations into the workflow to measure whether reviewers catch them. This borrows from a familiar idea: phishing simulation emails in security training work on the same principle. It creates a ground truth that is otherwise hard to get at runtime. The downside is that it requires careful design to avoid damaging trust or disrupting real work.

The questions that need answering are not just which signals to track. They include: how do we distinguish a behavioral change caused by the human from one caused by a model update? How do we set thresholds that are meaningful, not arbitrary? How can we best design workflows that support active reviewer engagement? 

What follows from this 

These are difficult questions and answering them will require both technical and behavioral research.  

But their existence does not argue against HITL as an oversight mechanism, which is often a reasonable and necessary control for AI systems. However, HITL should not be treated as a static safeguard simply because a person is present in the workflow. Like every other component of an AI system, its effectiveness can change over time and depends on the conditions under which it operates. 

If human oversight is the safeguard that makes these systems trustworthy, then it should be monitored and validated like every other safeguard in the system. This way we can ensure that the human is not simply “in the loop” but continues to provide meaningful oversight. 

HITL isn’t the only oversight mode, though. And for some AI use cases, it may not even be the right one. In our next post, we’ll look at a case where human-on-the-loop is a better fit than HITL, and why choosing the appropriate oversight mode matters just as much as making that mode work in practice. 

A Note on Transparency. Speaking of ethics principles, transparency is another one we take seriously. So, in the spirit of practicing what we preach: GenAI assisted in the creation of this blog post series. Its job? Giving feedback on structure, tone, and making suggestions for clarity and conciseness across multiple iterations. The image on top of the blog post was also modified by AI. The ideas, the arguments, and the accountability remain thoroughly human.
