entry.title: Deploying a Docker Model to SAP Generative AI Hub
entry.content:
Introduction


Deploying a custom model as a Docker container in SAP Generative AI Hub is a
practical approach when you want to expose your own inference logic as a scalable API
endpoint. This is especially useful when your model is packaged with custom runtime
dependencies, preprocessing or postprocessing logic, or when the model is not directly
available through standard managed options.


In this article, the focus is not on broader solution architecture, but on
the implementation flow required to take a trained model artifact, package it as a
Docker image, and deploy it through SAP Generative AI Hub so that it can be
consumed through an HTTP endpoint.

Why Deploy a Docker Model to SAP Generative AI Hub?


SAP Generative AI Hub provides access to a range of generative AI capabilities and
models through a governed enterprise platform. However, organizations often have AI
models that are not available as standard models in the platform.


For example, a company may have developed its own machine learning model for
customer classification, document processing, fraud detection, recommendation,
forecasting, or a domain-specific AI use case. Such a model may have been trained
internally using proprietary data and may need to be exposed as an API for consumption
by enterprise applications.


In these scenarios, the model can be packaged together with its inference logic and
dependencies into a Docker container and deployed through SAP AI Core, which
provides the underlying execution and lifecycle management capabilities used by SAP
Generative AI Hub.


This approach allows a custom model to be operated within the same broader
enterprise AI landscape while retaining control over the model runtime, dependencies,
and inference implementation. 

A simple example
Consider an organization that has trained a custom customer-intent classification
model using historical service interactions.
The model:
• Is not available in the standard model catalog.
• Has been trained using the organization's proprietary data.
• Requires a specific Python runtime and ML libraries.
• Contains custom preprocessing and postprocessing logic.
• Needs to be consumed by multiple enterprise applications.
Instead of rebuilding the model for every consuming application, the organization can
package the model and inference code into a Docker image and expose it through a
REST API.
The resulting architecture looks conceptually like this:
Trained Model → Docker Container → SAP AI Core → Deployed Inference Endpoint →
Enterprise Applications

The same approach can be used for many other custom ML models.

Typical Use Cases

Deploying a Dockerized model is particularly useful when the organization already has a
trained model and wants to make it available as a managed inference service.
Typical scenarios include:

1. Custom classification models
For example:
• Customer intent classification
• Lead or opportunity classification
• Document classification
• Risk or fraud classification
• Product categorization

The model can be packaged with its preprocessing and inference logic and exposed
through a standard REST endpoint.

2. Domain-specific machine learning models

Organizations may have models trained specifically on their business data, such as:
• Demand forecasting
• Customer churn prediction
• Recommendation models
• Anomaly detection
• Predictive maintenance
These models may not be available through a standard generative AI model catalog but
can still be operationalized through a containerized deployment.

3. Custom NLP or document-processing models
A model such as a custom NER, OCR, document classification, or text-processing
model can be packaged together with the required libraries and inference code.

4. Open-source or internally developed models
Organizations may want to operationalize an open-source model or an internally
developed model while maintaining control over the model runtime and dependencies.

5. Models with custom inference logic

A model may require more than simply sending an input and receiving an output. For
example, the inference service may perform:
Input validation → preprocessing → model inference → postprocessing → response
generation

Packaging these components into the Docker image provides a consistent runtime for
the complete inference workflow.

When Should You Choose a Docker-Based Model Deployment?

A Docker-based deployment is a good choice when you need to bring your own model
and runtime into an enterprise-managed AI environment.
Consider this approach when:
The model is not available as a standard model
If the model you need is not available through the models provided by the platform, a
custom Docker deployment provides a way to expose your own model as an inference
service.

You have a proprietary or domain-specific model
Organizations may have models trained using proprietary datasets or models
specifically designed for their business domain.
Examples include custom classification, recommendation, forecasting, anomaly
detection, or NLP models.


The model has specific runtime dependencies
Your model may require a particular Python version, ML framework, system library, or a
combination of dependencies that are difficult to reproduce in another runtime.
Docker allows the model and its runtime dependencies to be packaged together.


You require custom inference logic
The inference service may need to perform preprocessing, validation, postprocessing,
business rules, or other custom operations around the model.
Instead of exposing only the model itself, the complete inference implementation can
be packaged into the container.


You need control over compute resources
Different models have different resource requirements. A containerized deployment
allows the serving workload to be configured according to the model's CPU, memory,
and, where applicable, accelerator requirements.
Scaling parameters can also be configured according to expected workload.


You want to operationalize an existing ML model
If you already have a trained model and an inference implementation, containerizing it
can provide a relatively straightforward path to expose the model as a managed API
rather than rebuilding the model for a different serving environment.

When is a Docker-Based Model Deployment Not Necessary?


A Docker-based deployment is not necessarily the right choice for every AI use case.
You may not need this approach when:
• The required model is already available through the supported model offerings in
SAP Generative AI Hub.
• You only need standard LLM capabilities such as text generation, summarization,
classification, or embeddings and do not have a custom model to operate.
• Your requirement can be satisfied using an existing managed AI service without
maintaining your own inference container.
• The model does not require custom dependencies or inference logic.
• The additional operational responsibility of building, maintaining, securing, and
updating a container does not provide sufficient value for the use case.

Architecture

Prerequisites
• SAP BTP tenant with access to SAP Generative AI Hub and appropriate role
collections
• A trained model artifact (for example, model.pt)
• Docker installed locally and an account on a container registry (Docker Hub,
GitHub Container Registry, GitLab Container Registry, or similar)
• A Git repository to store the application code and YAML manifest
• Basic familiarity with Python (or your chosen runtime), REST APIs, and
containerization
• Personal access tokens or credentials for your Git and container registry
accounts


What You Will Build
• A simple inference service that loads your model and exposes a /predict
endpoint over HTTP
• A Docker image pushed to your container registry
• A Git-tracked YAML manifest that declares the application image and runtime
settings
• An application entry, configuration, and deployment in SAP Generative AI Hub
• An inference endpoint URL that can be consumed by authorized applications


What this article does not cover
This article is intentionally focused on the how-to steps for deployment. It does not go
into detailed solution architecture, model selection strategy, infrastructure sizing, or
comparative analysis of deployment options. Those topics can be explored separately if
needed but are outside the scope of this walkthrough.

Now let’s dive into the steps in details:

Build and push the docker image to a container registry:
• Below is an example of the commands required to create a docker file for a
python application.

One line explanation for each command:

Command

Purpose

FROM python:3.12-slim

Uses the Python 3.12 slim image as the base for the container.

WORKDIR /app

Sets /app as the current working directory inside the container.

COPY requirements.txt .

Copies the local requirements.txt file into the container's working directory.

RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

Installs all Python dependencies listed in requirements.txt during image build.

COPY . .

Copies all application files from the current local directory into the container.

CMD ["python", "main.py"]

Runs main.py when the container starts.

A useful way to remember them is:

  1. FROM → Base image
  2. WORKDIR → Where to work
  3. COPY → Copy files
  4. RUN → Execute build-time commands
  5. CMD → Execute run-time command (container startup)
  • Follow the steps below to create a docker image and push it to the docker container registry. Assuming your Docker Hub username is myuser, image name is myapp, and you're in the directory containing the Dockerfile.

Run the commands in terminal:

  • Build the Docker image
    • docker build -t myuser/myapp:latest .
  • Login to Docker Hub
    • docker login
  • Push the image to Docker Hub
    • docker push myuser/myapp:latest

Add new Docker/container registry credentials

Follow the path:

Login to SAP AI Launchpad

  1. SAP AI Core Administration
  2. Docker Registry Secrets
  3. Click Add
  4. Enter the Name for your docker registry and enter the credentials for your docker registry in below format:
    {

".dockerconfigjson":

"{\"auths\":

{\"YOUR_DOCKER_REGISTRY_URL\":

{\"username\":\"YOUR_DOCKER_USERNAME\",

\"password\":\"YOUR_DOCKER_ACCESS_TOKEN\"

}    }   }"  }

Create a Git-Tracked YAML Manifest

Create a YAML file that contains:

1. Metadata

  • Service name, description, scenario ID, and version.
  • Information displayed in SAP AI Launchpad and AI Core.

2. Deployment Configuration

  • Defines that the workload is a KServe-based serving application.
  • Configures autoscaling behavior (how the service scales up/down based on incoming requests).

3. Docker Registry Access

  • Specifies the Docker registry secret (imagePullSecrets) used to authenticate and pull the Docker image.

4.  Container Definition

  • Specifies the Docker image to run.
  • Defines the exposed application port.
  • Defines the startup command used to launch the application (e.g., FastAPI/Uvicorn).

5. Resource Scaling

  • Sets minimum and maximum replicas (number of running instances).
  • Controls availability and scalability of the service.

This file tells SAP AI Core:

"Deploy this Docker image as a continuously running API service, keep at least N instances running, scale when needed, and expose the application so external systems can send inference requests."

Attached document contains a Template of the YAML file. 

Link the Git Repository to SAP Generative AI Hub

Follow the below steps to link the Git repository to the Gen. AI Hub:

  • Login to the Gen AI Hub
  • Navigate to SAP AI Core Administration à Git Repositories
  • Click on “Add”
  • Maintain the
    • URL end point of the Git Repository
    • Name for this Git repository
    • User Name & Access Token

Create an Application Registry Entry

Follow the below steps to link the YAML file created in previous step to the Gen. AI Hub:

  1. Login to the Gen AI Hub
  2. Navigate to SAP AI Core Administration -> Applications
  3. Click on “Create”
  4. Maintain the
    • Application Name (Name for the new entry)
    • Repository (Select the Git Repository entry created in previous step)
    • Maintain the file path to the YAML file created in previous step

Create a Configuration for the Application

Follow the below steps to create configuration reference to the application created in previous steps:

  1. Login to the Gen AI Hub
  2. Click on Workspaces à Select a Resource Groups
  3. Click on ML Operations --> Configurations
  4. Click on “Create”
  5. Maintain the
    • Configuration Name (Name to the configuration)
    • Select the Scenario (Name to the application created in previous step)
    • Select the version from the drop-down value
    • Select the Executable value from the drop-down value
  6. Maintain the
    • Input Parameters (If parameters are defined)
    • Input Artifacts (If parameters are defined)

       7. Review and click on “Create”

Create a Deployment from the Configuration

Once the configuration is complete, create the deployment. Once the deployment is complete and successful, end point url is generated which can be used for calling from any application to make predictions.

entry.title: Smarter Slotting in SAP EWM: What If Products That Travel Together Could Live Together?
entry.content:
Smarter Slotting in SAP EWM: What If Products That Travel Together Could Live Together?

An idea for extending ML-based slotting with product affinity

Introduction

Warehouse slotting has always been about putting the right product in the right place. But as warehouses become more intelligent, perhaps the question should no longer stop there.

What if two products are both stored in the right area, but they are frequently picked together and located far apart?

From an individual product perspective, the slotting decision may be completely correct. From an order-picking perspective, however, there may still be room for improvement.

In my work around SAP EWM, I have often seen how a warehouse decision can look perfectly logical when we look at one product at a time. But warehouse operations rarely executed one product at a time. Pickers move through orders, and orders create relationships between products.

That made me think about whether we are sometimes optimizing the location of individual products without fully optimizing the journey created by the order.

This led me to an idea: could product affinity become another signal that complements SAP EWM’s existing Machine Learning–based slotting?

Not as a replacement for the existing slotting logic, but as another layer of intelligence on top of it.

I call this idea Smarter Neighbors.

SAP EWM can already use machine learning to answer an important warehouse question:

Where should this product live?

But there is another question warehouses deal with every day:

What products usually go together?

What SAP EWM Already Does

SAP EWM’s Slotting by Machine Learning is already a useful capability. Through SAP’s Intelligent Scenario Lifecycle Management (ISLM) framework, it can analyze warehouse and product data and propose storage parameters such as the Storage Type Indicator, Storage Section Indicator, and Putaway Control Indicator.

The idea is straightforward: instead of manually deciding how a product should be classified based on expected movement and characteristics, the model learns from existing warehouse data and recommends an appropriate storage concept.

That is a meaningful step forward.

But the question I started exploring is whether the product itself is only one part of the story.

Because a warehouse does not ultimately pick products in isolation.

It picks orders.

What If We Looked at the Relationship Between Products?

Consider two products, Product A and Product B.

Both are fast movers, so the ML model can correctly identify them and place them in the appropriate fast-pick area.

Now imagine that 70% of the orders containing Product A also contain Product B.

If A is located at one end of the fast-pick area and B is at the other, the picker still must walk between them.

Both products were individually slotted correctly.

But the relationship between them was not considered.

This is where product affinity becomes interesting.

Instead of asking only:

“How fast does this product move?”

We could also ask:

“Which other products does this product usually move with?”

Product affinity, or correlated slotting, uses historical order patterns to identify products that frequently occur together. Those relationships could then potentially be used to position products closer to each other.

The objective isn’t simply to find products that are popular. It is to understand which products repeatedly participate in the same warehouse journeys.

A Different Layer of Intelligence: “Smarter Neighbors”

I think of this idea as Smarter Neighbors.

The existing ML-based slotting model could continue deciding the type of location a product should have — for example, fast-pick, bulk, or slower-moving storage.

An additional affinity layer could then look at order history and help optimize the physical proximity of products within that broader zone.

In simple terms:

ML slotting could decide the neighborhood, while affinity could help decide the neighbors.

That distinction is important to me.

I would not want affinity to override the fundamental storage strategy. A product should not suddenly move to a completely different storage area simply because it is frequently ordered with another product.

Instead, affinity could act as an additional signal for optimizing placement within an appropriate storage concept.

This creates a two-level decision:

Storage strategy → Where should the product live?

Product affinity → Who should it live closer to?

How Could It Work?

The first step would be to analyze confirmed outbound order history and identify which products frequently appear on the same orders.

From this data, we could calculate an affinity score between products and identify strong relationships.

For example, if Product A and Product B repeatedly appear together across a significant number of orders, the system could recognize that relationship and consider it when determining their final placement.

The existing slotting logic would still determine the broader storage concept.

Affinity would then become another input when deciding where the product should ideally sit within that zone.

There is also an important rule for situations where the two signals disagree.

Suppose Product A is a very fast mover, while its strongest affinity partner, Product B, is a slow-moving product.

It probably would not make sense to move Product B into the fast-pick area simply because the two products are frequently ordered together.

So, my initial thinking would be simple:

Velocity and product characteristics determine the storage zone; product affinity helps optimize proximity within that zone.

This separation could also make the approach easier to govern. The warehouse can retain the existing storage logic while using affinity as a controlled optimization layer.

Why I Think of the Separation Matters

From a practical EWM perspective, I would be cautious about making this an automated relocation mechanism from day one.

A mathematically strong affinity relationship does not automatically mean that two products should be physically adjacent.

There may be other considerations:

  • Storage capacity
  • Replenishment frequency
  • Product dimensions and weight
  • Handling requirements
  • Hazardous-material restrictions
  • Equipment requirements
  • Temperature or storage conditions
  • Operational constraints
  • Warehouse supervisor experience

A model may identify a strong relationship between two products, but the warehouse still needs to decide whether that relationship is operationally meaningful.

That is why I see Smarter Neighbors as a recommendation layer first, rather than an autonomous relocation mechanism.

The system could identify the relationship, propose a placement adjustment, and allow warehouse operations to validate the recommendation before execution.

The Interesting Part: SAP Already Has Some of the Building Blocks

This is also why I think the idea is worth exploring from an SAP perspective.

SAP’s existing ML capabilities around EWM use the ISLM framework, while HANA’s Predictive Analysis Library (PAL) provides analytical capabilities that include association-rule mining such as Apriori-based algorithms.

Association-rule mining is designed to identify relationships and co-occurrence patterns in datasets.

And that is essentially what we are trying to understand here:

Which products tend to appear together?

So, this isn’t necessarily about inventing completely new technology.

It could be about applying existing analytical capability to another warehouse problem.

The interesting question is how such a capability could relate to the existing EWM slotting process in a way that remains practical, explainable, and operationally controlled.

Could This Become Another ML Signal for Slotting?

This is where I see an interesting product opportunity.

Today, intelligent slotting can largely be thought of at a product level:

  • How fast does the item move?
  • What are its physical characteristics?
  • What storage concept does it require?
  • What storage parameters should be assigned?

What if future intelligent slotting could consider another dimension:

How do products behave together in actual customer orders?

The recommendation could potentially move beyond simply saying:

Put Product A in Zone X.

It could say something more like:

Put Product A in Zone X, preferably closer to Products B and C because they frequently travel together.

That would introduce a different dimension of intelligence into slotting.

The system would not only understand the characteristics and movement of an individual product.

It would begin to understand the relationship between products within the order flow.

Where Would I Start with a Pilot?

I wouldn’t try this across an entire warehouse initially.

I’d start with an area where multi-line orders are common.

Potential candidates could include:

  • E-commerce
  • Kitting operations
  • Recurring B2B replenishment
  • Spare parts
  • Promotional product combinations

The pilot could compare the existing placement with an affinity-adjusted placement while keeping the underlying product classification unchanged.

The primary measurement could be simple:

Pick-path distance per order.

Other useful measurements could include picker travel time, lines picked per hour, order cycle time, and potentially congestion within the picking area.

But I will start with one simple question:

Did the affinity-adjusted placement reduce the distance the picker had to travel?

If product classification remains unchanged but average travel distance decreases, that would provide an early indication that the additional affinity layer is contributing real value.

I would also want the pilot to run under controlled conditions. Product relocation should not happen simply because an algorithm identifies a correlation. The recommendation should be reviewed against warehouse constraints and operational experience.

Why Affinity Could Need a Different Learning Cycle

There is another aspect of this idea that I find particularly interesting.

Product velocity may change gradually, while product relationships can change much faster.

A promotion can suddenly cause two products to appear together frequently.

A new bundle can create a new relationship.

Seasonality can change order patterns.

Customer behavior can shift.

A product that historically had little relationship with another product may suddenly become a frequent companion.

This suggests that affinity could potentially have its own shorter retraining or recalculation cycle, without constantly changing the underlying storage strategy.

The warehouse could therefore maintain a relatively stable storage classification while allowing proximity recommendations to respond more dynamically to changes in actual order behavior.

Is This Already Being Done?

The concept of affinity-based or correlated slotting isn’t new in warehousing.

Similar principles are already used in areas such as market-basket analysis, warehouse optimization, and order-picking research.

What I am particularly curious about is the SAP EWM context.

Has anyone experimented with using order co-occurrence or association-rule analysis alongside standard EWM slotting?

For example, could this be explored through:

  • A custom BAdI
  • A side-by-side model on SAP BTP
  • HANA PAL
  • Custom analytics
  • A recommendation service
  • Or even a simpler analysis feeding recommendations back into the product or warehouse master data?

I would be very interested to hear how others have approached this.

Perhaps someone has already implemented a similar concept in an EWM environment, even if it wasn’t explicitly called “affinity-based slotting.”

Conclusion: From Smarter Products to Smarter Relationships

For me, the interesting part of this idea is not whether we can build another machine-learning model.

The technology to identify relationships between products already exists.

The more interesting question is whether we can use that intelligence in a way that complements the warehouse processes and controls already built into SAP EWM.

A product can be correctly classified based on its movement, physical characteristics, and storage requirements — and still be part of an inefficient picking journey because the products it frequently travels with are located far away.

That is where I see the potential of Smarter Neighbors.

The existing ML-based slotting logic could continue answering:

Where does this product belong?

An affinity layer could add another question:

Who should this product live next to?

Maybe the next step in intelligent slotting isn’t only teaching SAP EWM where a product belongs.

Maybe it’s also teaching the system which products belong together.

entry.title: From AI Assistance to Human-on-the-Loop: A Compliance Detection Case Study
entry.content:
How can we step back from day-to-day decisions while staying firmly in control?

What if your compliance team could stop chasing false alarms and start focusing on what really matters? That’s exactly what happens when AI moves from being a helpful assistant to a tool that automatically handles routine cases.

In our second blog post, we explored a real-world example of human-in-the-loop (HITL) implementation from SAP: The Dispute Resolution Agent, illustrating what HITL oversight looks like in practice, and how it can fail. In our last blog post, we discussed the three failure modes of HITL – automation bias, decision fatigue, and cognitive overload – in more detail.

At SAP, human approval is mandatory in AI systems that carry a high risk of societal or personal harm. Curious about the details of SAP’s AI Ethics Assessment Process? Check it out in the SAP AI Ethics Handbook.

But what about low-risk AI use cases? Do they need the same level of oversight? Not always. For AI that does not pose serious risks to society or individuals, proper supervision is usually enough as long as the AI works as intended and works with sufficient accuracy.

Today, let’s look at “Compliance issues detection support”, an AI use case that shifts from AI assistance to a human-on-the-loop (HOTL) operating mode. If these terms sound unfamiliar, our introductory blog post is a great starting point.

This feature lives inside SAP Risk and Assurance Management, a solution that helps organizations maintain the internal controls and documented risks needed to protect financial and non-financial data, policies, and processes. Its job is to help compliance specialists flag issues either as confirmed, false positive, or inconclusive.

Why HOTL Fits This Use Case

Before diving in, let’s answer the obvious question: why not require human approval on every prediction?

Because these compliance predictions are low risk under SAP’s risk classification and fully reversible. Requiring sign-off on every single case would create bottlenecks without meaningfully reducing risk. HOTL strikes the right balance: speed and scale on routine cases, human judgment where it counts.

There’s another reason to prefer HOTL here. In our previous post, we saw how HITL can quietly degrade over time through automation bias, decision fatigue, and cognitive overload, especially when the volume of decisions is high. Requiring human approval on every low-risk compliance prediction wouldn’t just create bottlenecks; it would set up exactly the conditions in which HITL tends to fail. HOTL sidesteps that trap by reserving human judgment for the cases that really need it.

How AI Assists Humans with Compliance Detection

At first, the system predicts likely outcomes so specialists can prioritize which compliance issues to tackle first. The predicted conclusions only act as proposals. A human needs to set the conclusion manually and drive all necessary follow-up actions.

You might be wondering: why is this AI assistance and not HITL?

Let’s walk through the process. In step 1, the system displays issues along with predicted conclusions in the issue list:

Take a closer look, and you’ll see the predicted conclusion appears as a clickable link revealing deeper insights: the score, the thresholds, the model version, and the key influencers, in other words: the business data driving that prediction.

The prediction score is a numerical value the model calculates based on historical conclusions. The predicted conclusion itself falls into one of three buckets:

  • Confirmed: a real compliance issue
  • False positive: not a real compliance issue
  • Inconclusive: the score doesn’t clearly point either way

In step 2, a human steps in to investigate, and, if needed, adjust the conclusion and processing status. Users can also dig into the key influencers behind any specific decision to see how each factor contributed:

From here, AI takes a back seat. All follow-up actions are handled by a human. In a true HITL setup, the AI would wait for human approval and then trigger follow-up actions automatically. But that’s not what’s happening here.

How a Human Can Sit on the Loop

The model will learn from historic decisions and, once the customer decides that the model reached sufficient accuracy, the system can be configured to automatically determine a case outcome and trigger the appropriate follow-up actions:

When this happens, the conclusion still shows up as a link with all the supporting details behind it.

The best part? A human can override the decision at any time. And when the model isn’t confident, it flags the conclusion as inconclusive, sending it back to a human for manual review.

This is what sets this AI feature apart from a “human-out-of-the-loop” operating mode that would not allow for human intervention and post-hoc override.

Safety Nets Built In

If you have read our introductory blog post, then you know that Human-in-command (HIC) is SAP’s baseline principle: humans always retain ultimate authority over AI systems, including the ability to oversee an AI system’s overall activity and to decide when and how the system should be used. Here’s how that principle shows up in this feature:

Pre-deployment validation. Model performance can be inspected before deployment, so the system is only used once it is ready.

Manual permissions elevation. No automated decision-making takes place until a human chooses to run the system in this mode.

Transparency at the core. AI decisions are clearly marked as such and can be reviewed by users.

Insights through explainability. Every predicted conclusion is explainable: users can inspect the score, thresholds, model version, and key influencers driving the decision.

Human override, always possible. No decision is ever locked in. Compliance specialists can change any conclusion at any time, no matter how confident the model is.

Automatic escalation. Low-confidence cases are automatically routed for manual review, reducing false positives and false negatives.

Together, these safeguards ensure that efficiency does not come at the cost of oversight.

Wrapping Up

Compliance work is too important to slow down with unnecessary approvals, but too important to fully hand over to AI, either. Human-on-the-loop offers the sweet spot: AI handles the routine, humans handle the exceptions, and the system allows for human overrides.

So far, we’ve looked at oversight one use case at a time. But what happens when an organization runs not one, not two, but hundreds of AI agents at once, each operating in a different mode? In our final post of the series, we’ll zoom out to the Autonomous Enterprise and ask what human oversight has to look like when it operates at ecosystem scale.

A Note on Transparency. Speaking of ethics principles, transparency is another one we take seriously. So, in the spirit of practicing what we preach: GenAI assisted in the creation of this blog post series. Its job? Giving feedback on structure, tone, and making suggestions for clarity and conciseness across multiple iterations. The image on top of the blog post was generated by AI. The ideas, the arguments, and the accountability remain thoroughly human.

entry.title: ABAP AI's Three Circles in Practice
entry.content:
ABAP AI's Three Circles in Practice (Series 3, Part 5: Clean Core + AI)

By Deepa Dorairaj | SAP AI Solution Architect | Series 3, Part 5 of 6 | Published September 2026

TL;DR: SAP frames ABAP AI as three concentric circles — ABAP Cloud core, developer AI tooling, and agents — and says they "coexist and reinforce each other." That's easy to nod along to and hard to picture. This part walks the consolidation case from Part 4 back through all three circles, showing where an agent did the finding, where AI tooling did the building, and where a human still had to make the one call none of it could make for her.

The model, in Liénard's own framing

In an August 2026 interview with SAP News, Sonja Liénard — SVP and head of ABAP platform, and head of ABAP AI — laid out the vision she uses internally:

"ABAP Cloud is at the center, as the modern, clean-core variant of our language for long-term stability. The second circle is the ABAP AI layer: developer tools for code explanation, code generation, and ghost texting. The outer circle is comprised of AI agents, a network of specialized agents for complex and multi-step tasks such as transformation, migration, and quality validation."

Three layers, one direction of travel: stable core, assisted authoring, autonomous orchestration. Liénard's own qualifier is the part worth sitting with — "the circles coexist and reinforce each other." Not replace. Reinforce. The rest of this piece is what that actually looks like on a real object, not a slide.

The case: back to the three Z-programs

Part 4 left off with a decision, not just a diagram. Three Z-programs — same domain, inconsistent parameter names, duplicated logic — got consolidated into one CAP service: one entity, one function branching internally on method, properly typed. That decision didn't happen in one circle. It happened across all three, in sequence.

Outer circle — an agent found the debt.


Part 2 of this series covered ATC as clean core's quality gate — SAP Note 3565942, the Kernseife extensibility checks, the Clean Core Levels A–D. What Part 2 didn't cover is that a human doesn't have to run that assessment manually anymore. SAP's Mass Clean Core Adoption Agent, announced alongside the custom code migration agent this year, scans exactly this kind of landscape: it identifies clean-core ATC violations, fixes what it can fix outright, and — for anything that needs judgment — returns a structured recommendation instead of guessing. Three Z-programs with overlapping logic and no released-API path is precisely the "needs judgment" case. The agent's output wasn't "here's your new service." It was "here are three violations that look related — a human should look at this together."

That's the outer circle doing what Liénard describes it doing: multi-step, structured, but explicitly handing off the decision it isn't built to make.

The decision itself — nobody's circle.


Consolidating three programs into one service, choosing the entity shape, deciding what the function's internal branching should look like — that's architecture. None of the three circles claims to do this, and SAP doesn't pretend otherwise. Liénard's own framing of what AI frees up is "decisions regarding business logic and architecture, as well as verifying quality." The agent's flag started the process; a person's judgment shaped the service.

Middle circle — AI tooling built it.


Once the shape was decided, the actual writing is where the second circle earns its place. Two capabilities do the heavy lifting here, both shipped as part of Joule for Developers, ABAP AI capabilities: code explanation and ghost text (SAP's term for inline, accept-as-you-type code generation). Code explanation is what makes it safe to consolidate in the first place — before merging three programs, you need to actually understand what each one's edge cases were doing, not just what they were named. Ghost text is what makes writing the consolidated version fast rather than tedious: typed intent, generated implementation, still reviewed line by line before it ships. SAP's own design principle for these tools, stated in their Sapphire 2026 announcement, is to explain and understand existing code before proposing changes — protecting the investment already made in the custom code, not just replacing it wholesale.

Center circle — where it had to land.


The consolidated service is only worth building if it lives somewhere stable. That's the center circle's job, and it's the one that doesn't get a dramatic moment — ABAP Cloud is the boring, load-bearing constraint that made everything upstream of it accountable to something. The service consumes released APIs, not internal tables. It sits inside the debt register from Part 4, not outside it. If the core weren't clean to begin with, there'd be nothing stable for the agent to scan or the tooling to generate against — this is the part Part 1 of this series argued from the other direction.

What the roadmap says about where this is headed

This isn't a one-off case study; it's the current shape of a fast-moving roadmap. As of Q2 2026, the ABAP MCP server shipped for both Eclipse and VS Code, opening agentic ABAP development to any MCP-compatible client — this is what Part 3 walked through directly with the Custom Code Migration Agent. Alongside the migration agent, SAP shipped the Mass Clean Core Adoption Agent used above and a Web Dynpro-to-Fiori modernization agent for a different class of legacy debt. A second agent, focused specifically on clean-core transformation, is planned for Q3 2026, with continued work on multi-agent orchestration through the rest of the year. SAP's own early evaluations target a 40% efficiency gain in custom code transformation work — a number worth watching for independent validation as more of these agents reach general availability, not taking at face value yet.

The honest gap in the model

The three-circles diagram implies clean handoffs — agent flags, tooling builds, core absorbs. The real sequence had a fourth step wedged in the middle that belongs to none of the circles: a person deciding what "consolidated" should actually mean for this domain. SAP's framing accounts for this implicitly — Liénard's answer about what AI frees up isan admission that architecture and business logic decisions stay human. But it's worth saying plainly, because it's the difference between "agents do clean core" and what's actually happening, which is closer to: agents surface the debt, tooling removes the friction of fixing it, and the core stays the one thing that has to be true before either of the other two circles means anything.

Part 6 closes this series by tying that center circle to something more concrete than "stable" — how a clean core is what makes agent governance actually enforceable, through the MCP Gateway and AI Agent Hub verification, rather than a compliance slide.

If you've run an agent-assisted clean-core assessment on your own landscape: did the agent's flag match where your own architects would have looked first, or did it surface something you'd have missed?

entry.title: Smart Report - Example with VA05N (List of Sales Orders)
entry.content:
I’ve designed numerous processes, reports, and APIs. However, traditional development often ties solutions tightly to specific user requirements, which limits flexibility. My goal has always been to build open, configurable solutions where users can adjust behavior through settings rather than code changes.

A recurring challenge remains: How do we design systems that give users maximum flexibility in how they query and retrieve information from the backend?

With the emergence of LLMs and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), this challenge is becoming easier to solve. By exposing SAP backend services through MCP, users can interact with SAP data using natural language, and the LLM can generate meaningful responses dynamically.

To explore this idea further, I experimented with enabling LLM‑based querying on report data — essentially creating a Smart Report concept. For testing, I used the SAP VA05N report, surfaced its data through a SAPUI5 application, and added intelligent features powered by LLMs. This approach demonstrates how traditional SAP reports can evolve into flexible, conversational, and insight‑driven tools.

The Architecture         :

The Output     :

SAP Back-end Designed :

Designed and implemented the ZREPORT_RAG database table to persist user RAG session details, enabling comprehensive session logging and traceability. The solution also includes logic to identify and remove any existing active session before creating a new one, ensuring data consistency and preventing duplicate or stale session records.

 

Developed the class ZCL_REPORT_CORE to centralize the core processing logic for the application, including the primary methods GET_VA05N_DATA, CREATE_RAG, and GET_RAG. To retrieve the executed report output efficiently, the implementation leverages the standard SAP class CL_SALV_BS_RUNTIME_INFO, specifically its GET_DATA_REF method, enabling seamless access to ALV report data post‑execution. Additional handling was incorporated to manage data extraction, transformation, and preparation for downstream RAG generation within the application workflow.

Subsequently, an OData service ZREPORTS was developed using the SEGW transaction. Two entities were modeled: raginfo, backed by the ZREPORT_RAG table, and va05n, based on the SVBMTV_TRVOG structure.

The corresponding entity methods—RAGINFOSET_CREATE_ENTITY, RAGINFOSET_GET_ENTITY, and VA05NSET_GET_ENTITYSET—were redefined to integrate the core logic from ZCL_REPORT_CORE, invoking CREATE_RAG, GET_RAG, and GET_VA05N_DATA respectively. This enabled the creation and retrieval of RAG session logs as well as the delivery of VA05N report data to the SAPUI5 application.

Ollama

Deployed the Ollama instance inside a Docker container to ensure a clean, reproducible, and easily maintainable environment for local model experimentation.

After the deployment, installed a set of models tailored for coding assistance, general reasoning, and text‑embedding workflows:

  • qwen2.5-coder:latest — optimized for code generation, debugging, and developer‑focused tasks.
  • llama3.1:latest — a versatile general‑purpose model suitable for reasoning, drafting, and broader language tasks.
  • nomic-embed-text:latest — used for generating high‑quality text embeddings, ideal for semantic search, RAG pipelines, and similarity scoring.

Together, these models provide a balanced setup for development: strong coding support, reliable general LLM capabilities, and efficient embedding generation for retrieval‑augmented applications.

Report Analysis Api:

 

Developed a middleware api with following services:

/api/v1/report/session :

Used to store report data—both records and column definitions—into the DuckDB instance. DuckDB’s columnar storage and fast analytical capabilities make this endpoint ideal for capturing structured data that will later be queried, embedded, or analyzed using Ollama models.

/api/v1/report/session/all :

Fetches all currently available report sessions along with their associated metadata. This allows the system to quickly list active datasets stored in DuckDB.

/api/v1/report/session/{session_id} :

Deletes a specific session using its unique session ID. Removing outdated or unnecessary sessions helps maintain a clean DuckDB environment and ensures that Ollama models operate only on relevant datasets during query generation or embedding workflows.

/api/v1/report/qa :

Processes a query against a selected session and returns a formatted, model‑generated response. This endpoint typically uses DuckDB to retrieve the relevant data and then leverages Ollama models—such as qwen2.5‑coder, llama3.1, or nomic‑embed‑text—to perform reasoning, generate answers, or produce embeddings for RAG‑style responses.

/api/v1/report/getForecast :

Generates forward‑looking time‑series predictions by retrieving historical date–value data based on passing into formated date and value details, and applying high‑performance forecasting models from the StatsForecast Python library. Once the endpoint extracts and prepares the dataset, it leverages AutoARIMA to automatically identify the optimal ARIMA configuration based on temporal patterns, and AutoETS to model trend and seasonality using exponential smoothing. These complementary models allow the system to produce accurate forecasts for the specified horizon, while DuckDB ensures fast analytical retrieval and preprocessing. The endpoint can also optionally pair the numerical output with an Ollama model to provide narrative explanations or contextual insights, creating a lightweight yet powerful forecasting workflow suitable for analytical reporting and decision support.

The Front-end:

Developed a SAPUI5 application by using the OData backend service and Report Analysis Middleware API.

On load, RAGINFOSET_GET_ENTITY call to fetch latest generated user specific session details from SAP system and store into model variable.

Then on load of view, VA05NSET_GET_ENTITYSET service call to fetch all VA05N report data and display into smart table as below :

 

 

The table toolbar provides two key options

  1. Activate Smart Report and
  2. Chat

that work together to enable AI‑driven analysis. When the user selects Activate Smart Report, the current table view, including all visible fields, is sent to DuckDB by triggering the /api/v1/report/session endpoint; before creating this new session, the system deletes any previously stored session for that user to prevent stale or outdated data from influencing query generation, ensure the AI always works with the latest table snapshot, and maintain a clean one‑session‑per‑user workflow. Once the new session is successfully stored in DuckDB, the Chat option becomes active, allowing the user to ask questions against the freshly loaded dataset and receive model‑generated responses based on the most current information.

The system shows the user’s request in the chat area in a clean, easy‑to‑read format, just like a normal messaging app :

 

Details available into back-end system (VA05N T-Code 😞

 

Added a few more features related to the tabular data, as shown in the screen below.

 

 

At the top of any table‑based response, users can switch how the data is shown—either as a table or as an analytics view. For analytics, they can choose Bar, Line, Area, or Pie charts to better understand the information. These options are available only when the response contains tabular data.

Added another feature specifically for Date‑and‑Value datasets that allows users to generate forecasts or time‑series projections for up to 10 future periods.

For example, in the scenario below, the system calculates the total net value based on the “created‑on” dates and then applies a forecast to generate the next five future periods.

All program and logic details are available into :

https://github.com/ipravir/Smart-Report

This solution is built on an SAP EHP8 system and uses a local Ollama model, which is perfectly suitable for development, testing, and proving the overall concept. Moving to the SAP AI Core LLM service in the future can make responses faster, improve performance under heavy workloads, and provide better reliability as the application grows. The project also updates SAP ABAP syntax based on the system and kernel version, using newer and more efficient language features to improve runtime performance and maintainability.

Happy Learning 😀

entry.title: Governance at Scale: Why a Clean Core Is What Makes Agent Governance Enforceable
entry.content:
Governance at Scale: Why a Clean Core Is What Makes Agent Governance Enforceable (Series 3, Part 6: Clean Core + AI — Series Finale)

By Deepa Dorairaj | SAP AI Solution Architect | Series 3, Part 6 of 6 (Series Finale) | Published September 2026

TL;DR: SAP now ships two real governance mechanisms for agentic AI: MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite, which turns APIs into governed, policy-enforced tools; and AI Agent Hub, which discovers, assesses, and verifies every agent, LLM, and MCP server in a tenant. Both work by reasoning about a tool's surface — what it exposes, what it does, what it's allowed to touch. That reasoning is only possible when the surface is documented and stable. This closes the series by showing why a clean core isn't a separate initiative from agent governance — it's the thing that makes governance able to say something true.

Two governance layers, one shared requirement

MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite is the runtime control plane. It aggregates tools from SAP APIs, non-SAP APIs, integration flows, and external MCP servers into a single governed entry point, enforcing authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and payload protection on every call. The part worth noticing: API specifications are automatically translated into MCP schema and augmented with natural-language semantics, so an agent understands not just a tool's structure but what it's for — no manual schema translation, no hardcoding. Existing RBAC, rate limits, and monitoring carry forward into the agentic layer rather than getting rebuilt from scratch.

AI Agent Hub is the inventory and trust layer, built on SAP LeanIX. It auto-discovers agents, LLMs, and MCP servers across SAP, Microsoft, Google, AWS, and now ServiceNow and SAP AI Core, then runs structured governance assessments capturing risk rating, build type, and compliance mappings. Every asset enters unverified; a formal workflow marks it verified, rejected, or left unverified, with the badge then read by Joule Studio at runtime to decide which agents are approved for production, and by SAP Integration Suite to decide which MCP servers developers are allowed to use. As one SAP engineering write-up put it, this "ensures that nothing ships into production without a verified governance record." Q3 2026 additions bring identity management through SAP Cloud Identity Services and session-level observability on top.

Different layers, same underlying move: both convert a tool into something with a legible surface — declared inputs, declared scope, declared behavior — and then reason about that surface. Auto-translating a schema, assessing a risk rating, deciding whether to badge something as verified: all of it depends on the tool actually having a surface worth reasoning about.

Where that requirement breaks

Go back to the three Z-programs from Part 4, before consolidation. Modified internal tables. No released API. Parameter names that meant different things in each program despite doing similar work. Try to run either governance mechanism against that, honestly:

MCP Gateway can still technically wrap it — expose something as an MCP tool. But the auto-generated schema is only as good as what it's translating, and there's no released API contract underneath to translate faithfully. The natural-language semantics SAP's engine attaches would be describing implementation detail, not a documented interface, because there isn't one.

AI Agent Hub can still discover it and run an assessment. But a risk rating and compliance mapping are only meaningful relative to a documented scope. Verifying a tool whose actual access pattern is "reads and writes to whatever internal tables this Z-program happens to touch" isn't verification — it's a badge attached to a shrug. This is the same gap the EU AI Act's August 2026 enforcement deadline makes concrete for Finance, HR, and Procurement processes: documented audit trails and verifiable access controls aren't optional there, and neither mechanism can produce either against an undocumented surface.

Where it doesn't

Now run the same two mechanisms against the consolidated CAP service from Part 4 and Part 5 — the one built via ABAP AI's second circle, checked against a debt register, consuming only released APIs from an ABAP Cloud core. MCP Gateway's schema translation has something real to translate: one entity, one function, properly typed, with a defined contract. AI Agent Hub's assessment has something real to assess: a scope that's actually documented, a compliance mapping that maps to something that exists. The verification badge means what it claims to mean, because the thing underneath it can support the claim.

This is the throughline the whole series has been building toward. Part 1 argued clean core became a precondition for reliable AI reasoning. Parts 2 through 5 showed what building and governing toward that precondition actually looks like — the ATC-based assessment, the CAPM governance patterns, the three-circles model in practice. This closing piece is the reason all of it mattered beyond code quality: governance infrastructure can only govern what it can describe, and clean core is what makes an enterprise landscape describable in the first place.

Clean core isn't a 2026 initiative that fades once agentic AI stops being the newest architecture pattern. It's the infrastructure discipline every future wave — agents now, whatever replaces agents next — is going to keep depending on, for exactly this reason: nothing downstream can verify, govern, or trust what it can't first see clearly.

If you're rolling out AI Agent Hub or MCP Gateway against your own landscape: has verification surfaced gaps you already suspected, or has it found something in your custom code that genuinely surprised you?

entry.title: When Agents Multiply: Human Oversight in the Autonomous Enterprise
entry.content:
When Agents Multiply: Human Oversight in the Autonomous Enterprise

  How can we jump into this new adventure safely?

When we started this blog post series, we asked a hard question: how do we keep humans meaningfully involved as AI systems get more autonomous every day? Today, that question is more urgent than ever. SAP’s vision of the Autonomous Enterprise promises that AI assistants and agents take on end-to-end execution of routine processes. But autonomy and oversight are in constant tension: the more the system decides on its own, the harder it becomes to keep humans genuinely in control. So how does that tension get resolved?

The Role of Humans in the Autonomous Enterprise

It’s tempting to think that as AI gets better, oversight becomes optional. That’s the wrong conclusion. More autonomy means more surface area for things to go wrong. Subtle drift, cascading errors, decisions that compound across processes. Sounds familiar? In our very first blog post, we explained how a single error can propagate across multiple systems. That shows that human oversight is nothing we can discard when AI matures.

And that’s why SAP’s AI Ethics Assessment Process (read more in SAP’s AI Ethics Handbook) stays the same, even in the age of autonomous enterprises: every AI use case, including agentic AI, is assessed for its impact and ethical risks. In earlier posts, we saw human-in-the-loop (HITL) in action with the Dispute Resolution Agent and human-on-the-loop (HOTL) in action with Compliance Issues Detection Support. Each mode fit its use case because of its specific risk profile: If an AI use case carries serious ethical risk, we need a human to approve every consequential action. For AI with lower or more contained risk, humans supervise operation and intervene only when needed. And in all cases, the human-in-command (HIC) principle remains: humans retain ultimate authority, even when they aren’t clicking approve on every step. This includes the ability to oversee an AI system’s overall activity and to decide when and how the system should be used. The Autonomous Enterprise doesn’t mean that we leave all this behind and only deploy “human-out-of-the-loop” systems.

You may have heard SAP describe the target state of the Autonomous Enterprise as "human in the lead." It’s worth pausing on this phrase, because it’s easy to mistake it for yet another oversight mode alongside HITL, HOTL, and HIC. Human in the lead sits at a different level of abstraction: it’s the organizational and strategic stance that says people retain accountability, judgment, and strategic direction, while AI executes the routine within governed boundaries. Think of it as the umbrella under which the oversight modes operate. A single Autonomous Enterprise deployment can follow human in the lead overall while running some agents in HITL, others in HOTL, and all of them under the baseline principle of HIC.

Also from a regulatory point of view, we cannot entirely drop human oversight. The EU AI Act explicitly mandates human oversight for high-risk AI systems: humans must be able to understand the system’s capabilities, monitor its operation, interpret its output, and intervene when needed. Importantly, the EU AI Act holds the provider of the AI system responsible for ensuring this oversight is effective. But it’s not enough to build oversight capabilities into the AI; organizations deploying autonomous agents need trained people to exercise oversight effectively in practice. Which is where the challenge of the Autonomous Enterprise becomes concrete.

Training Human Oversight Personnel

In our previous blog post on the pitfalls of HITL designs, we have seen that HITL can overwhelm humans with too many complex decisions to approve at once, and that there’s a tendency in humans to over-rely on AI output (automation bias).

Here’s an uncomfortable truth: If we do not meaningfully include the very humans that are to oversee the system, then we don’t have effective human oversight measures in place. Moreover, as AI agents get more capable, the skills required to oversee them shift too: from 'checking outputs' to 'understanding behavior patterns,' 'spotting drift,' and 'making judgment calls about acceptable risk.' The best oversight tooling in the world is useless if the people using it are not trained to know what to look for.

Take 'spotting drift.' In practice, it means a compliance specialist who looks at a dashboard notices that an agent’s false-positive rate has crept up 2% over the last quarter and judges whether that’s noise, seasonality, or a real problem. 'Making judgment calls about acceptable risk' means being able to look at a behavior mining report and decide whether a newly observed pattern is a bug, a feature, or a red flag.

These aren’t tool skills, and you can’t train them with an online click-through tutorial. They’re judgment skills, and they develop the way judgment always develops: through regular exposure to real cases, mentorship from more experienced colleagues, and enough time on the job to build genuine pattern recognition.

When organizations skip this investment, oversight becomes theatre: dashboards get watched but not understood, exceptions get approved without scrutiny, and “human-in-the-loop” becomes a compliance checkbox rather than a genuine safeguard. Which is why any serious commitment to human oversight must include a serious commitment to the people doing the oversight.

How to Centrally Oversee AI Agents

Human oversight in the Autonomous Enterprise isn’t just a principle. In our previous blog post on HITL, we could see how SAP’s Dispute Resolution Agent is shipped with bespoke HITL controls that effectively mitigate the ethical risks that stem from its use.

However, with an increasing number of AI agents running in autonomous enterprises, we must find ways to manage thousands of agents operating continuously across the enterprise. Which is why we need to enforce human oversight centrally with monitoring dashboards and traceability features that allow for HOTL and HIC.

SAP AI Agent Hub is designed as a command center to provide AI governance organization-wide. And here’s how it translates oversight from theory into practice:

Are my agents doing what they should? Production dashboards let you monitor sessions, goal completion, and tool call accuracy across every agent, with the ability to drill into specifics when something looks off. Without this bird’s-eye view, problems tend to surface only when they’ve already caused damage: a customer complains, a report doesn’t add up, a downstream process breaks. A production dashboard shifts oversight from reactive to proactive. You see the agent that suddenly starts failing 15% of its tool calls before someone downstream notices.

How is this agent behaving? Agent behavior mining visualizes how agents execute tasks across business processes, surfacing patterns that would otherwise stay hidden. Individual agents can pass every test in isolation and still develop problematic patterns once they’re operating at scale. For example, an agent might technically complete tasks correctly but consistently route edge cases to the wrong queue, or quietly start favoring certain data sources over others. These patterns don’t show up in individual session logs, they only become visible when you can see behavior across many sessions. Behavior mining turns invisible drift into something you can spot and address.

What exactly happened in this session? Full traceability lets you inspect the execution flow: tool calls, response times, memory usage, and health status at every step. When something goes wrong (and eventually, something always does), the difference between a quick fix and a week-long investigation is whether you can reconstruct exactly what the agent did and why. Traceability is what makes post-hoc human oversight possible: it lets a specialist look at a flagged case, follow the agent’s reasoning step by step, and decide whether the outcome was a one-off glitch, a systematic problem, or actually correct behavior that just looked odd. Without it, you’re left guessing, and guessing is not oversight.

One honest caveat before we move on: the field is still working out what good oversight looks like at ecosystem scale. Tools like the Agent Hub represent the current state of the art, but we don’t yet have validated frameworks for questions like: How many agents can one human meaningfully supervise? What behavioral signals reliably predict emerging problems across an agent fleet? How do we know when centralized oversight itself has degraded? These are open questions in both research and practice.

Automation Has Limits. So Does Delegation.

When we started this series, we talked about what can go wrong when AI acts without human judgment. We learned that risks, such as an agent misinterpreting user intent, optimizing the wrong objective, or reinforcing historical bias, can lead to serious harm, whether that might be financial, reputational, or, most importantly, personal and societal.

In this series, we have seen how high-risk AI can be governed with explicit human approval steps, and how less-risky AI might be sufficiently governed with the possibility to override AI output and human approval for edge cases. This blog post explained why we need tools like the Agent Hub: Not because the individual agents are unsafe, but because we must keep track of hundreds of agents, each operating in a different mode.

To be clear: Tools like SAP’s AI Agent Hub don’t solve human oversight. They enable it. Falling into technological solutionism, believing that we can adopt a fancy tool and call it a day, is an easy trap. But the hardest parts of oversight remain fundamentally human responsibilities: deciding which oversight mode fits which agent, training people to spot problems, deciding when to override the system and when to trust it. AI can automate the routine. It cannot, and should not, automate accountability.

On the other hand: We cannot push all the responsibility to humans and keep our hands off any decisions that the AI we developed has proposed. We know about the pitfalls and limitations of HITL, so we also know that wrong AI output is not always corrected by humans, even if the responsibility and accountability lie officially with them.

In the end, it is clearly a sociotechnical system, so we must find the right balance, which is: the point where AI handles what it does best and humans stay accountable for what only humans can decide. This is what makes the Autonomous Enterprise deliver on its promise. Not autonomy for its own sake, but autonomy that is well-calibrated.

If there’s one message we hope you take from this series, it’s this: human oversight isn’t a feature you add to AI systems. It’s how you design them, deploy them, and monitor them. The Autonomous Enterprise makes that discipline harder and more important than ever.

A Note on Transparency. Speaking of ethics principles, transparency is another one we take seriously. So, in the spirit of practicing what we preach: GenAI assisted in the creation of this blog post series. Its job? Giving feedback on structure, tone, and making suggestions for clarity and conciseness across multiple iterations. The image on top of the blog post was also modified by AI. The ideas, the arguments, and the accountability remain thoroughly human.
