⏲Estimated reading time: 15 min

 

What You Will Get from This Blog

Imagine two opportunities with the same seller-entered probability.

One has a strong Machine Learning score. The other has a significantly lower score and a declining score trend.

Which one should the sales manager inspect first?

The score is not the answer. It is a signal that helps sellers and managers know where to look next.

This is where Lead and Deal Scoring in SAP Sales Cloud Version 2 can add value: not by replacing seller judgment, but by adding a predictive, data-driven perspective to sales prioritization and decision-making.

In this blog, Lead Scoring refers to predictive scoring used to prioritize leads, while Deal Scoring refers to the Opportunity Scoring capability within SAP Deal Intelligence. We will look beyond simply activating these features and focus on a question customers and consultants frequently ask:

What sits behind the score — and what makes it meaningful and trustworthy?

We will explore how scoring works in Sales Cloud V2, including the different model approaches, data and readiness requirements, Lead and Opportunity use cases, common roadblocks, adoption best practices, and practical guidance for consultants assessing customer readiness.

 

 

Why Lead & Deal Scoring Matters

Sales organizations rarely struggle because they have too few leads or opportunities.

The challenge is deciding where limited seller and manager attention should go first.

For Lead Scoring, the goal is to help sellers prioritize prospects with higher potential for conversion.

For Deal Scoring, the score provides an additional predictive signal to help sellers and managers identify opportunities that deserve attention, challenge pipeline assumptions, and focus their sales efforts more effectively.

Typical business questions include:

  • Which leads should sellers contact first?
  • Which opportunities deserve additional management attention?
  • Are seller-maintained probabilities consistent with what historical sales data suggests?
  • Which deals may require investigation before the next forecast meeting?

The business value therefore comes from better prioritization, earlier intervention, and more informed sales conversations — rather than from the score itself.

 

 

How Does the Machine Learning Model Work Behind the Scenes?

Native or SAP-RPT? An Important V2 Difference

A useful way to understand scoring in SAP Sales Cloud V2 is to first distinguish between the two model approaches available for Lead and Deal Scoring: Native and SAP-RPT.

The Native model is customer-specific. It is trained on the customer’s historical Lead/Opportunity data and follows the traditional Machine Learning lifecycle:

SAP Sales Cloud V2 also introduces SAP-RPT (Relational Pretrained Transformer) as an alternative model option. Unlike the Native approach, SAP-RPT is a pretrained foundation model for structured business data. It uses in-context learning to generate predictions without requiring a customer-specific model to be trained.

This makes SAP-RPT particularly relevant for customers whose historical dataset is not sufficient to train a Native model.

 

 

NATIVE

SAP-RPT

Model Approach

Customer-specific model trained on historical sales data

Pretrained relational foundation model

Training

Requires customer historical data and model training

Uses in-context learning; no customer-specific model training required

Best Suited For

Customer with sufficient representative historical data

Customer with limited data for native training

Seller Insight

Score plus key factors and scoring insights

Opportunity score only

Key Factors

Available

Not available

For customers coming from C4C / Sales Cloud V1, this is an important difference: V2 is no longer limited to the traditional customer-trained scoring approach.

At the time of writing, SAP-RPT model selection is documented as restricted availability and should therefore be validated for the applicable customer tenant before implementation.

 

What Data is Behind the Score?

For a Native model, historical business data is the foundation of the prediction. The model learns patterns from previous outcomes and applies those patterns to current Leads or Opportunities.

For Deal Scoring, SAP documents major input categories such as:

  • Sales Representative performance.
  • Sales attributes, such as sales area, priority, status, and sales cycle.
  • Deal lifecycle.

Because the Native model is customer-specific, two organizations may obtain different scoring behavior because their historical sales processes, data, and outcomes are different.

For Lead Scoring, SAP Sales Cloud V2 documents data points including:

  • Open date/quarter
  • Priority
  • Region/Channel/Organizational attributes
  • Origin/Source
  • Account
  • Sales and marketing activities
  • Lead owner historical performance

This reinforces an important principle:

The model learns from the sales process represented in CRM data — not necessarily from the process described in the sales methodology.

If outcomes, priorities, sales phases, sources, activities, or other relevant information are inconsistently maintained, those inconsistencies also become part of the training data.

Therefore, for both models, before relying on lead / Opportunity scores and its relevant insights, assess whether the historical CRM data reflects the sales process you want the models to learn - check the consistency of lead / opportunities outcomes, priorities, sources, activities, and ownership, then validate the scores with sales teams against real conversion patterns. More info/guidance will be taken on the Prerequisites and Readiness: Good Scoring Starts Before Training chapter as part of this blog. 

 

Training Is Different from Scoring

For the Native model, training and scoring are two separate activities.

Training uses historical customer data to create the predictive model. Once the model has been trained, validated, and activated, scoring applies that model to current business records.

Therefore, changing an Opportunity or Lead does not retrain the Native model. The updated information is evaluated during subsequent scoring.

SAP-RPT works differently. Because it is pretrained and uses in-context learning, it does not require the same customer-specific model training process.

This distinction is particularly important when discussing data readiness, model selection, and data-volume requirements with customers.

 

How Should We Interpret the Score?

Lead and Deal scores are returned on a 0–99 scale.

One detail is especially important when explaining Deal Scoring to customers:

93 ≠ 93% probability

A score of 93 does not mean a guaranteed 93% probability of winning. Treat it as a predictive signal to be interpreted together with Key Factors, score trend and business context.

SAP describes Opportunity Score as a relative score. For example, an opportunity scored at 93 has a better predicted chance of winning than one scored at 82.

The score should therefore be treated as an additional predictive signal — not as a replacement for the seller’s knowledge of the customer or the current deal context.

 

Understanding Key Factors and Score Trend

With the Native model, SAP provides additional insights to help users understand the prediction.

Dynamic Key Factors are influencing factors that can change during the lifecycle of the Lead or Opportunity. They are separated into the most influencing factors, shown in green, and the least influencing factors, shown in red.

Static Key Factors follow the same principle but represent factors that do not change.

For each category, SAP displays up to three most influencing and three least influencing factors, with a maximum of six factors displayed in each Key Factor section.

Score Trend provides a graphical representation of how the score has evolved over time, while the score delta shows the change compared with the previous score.

Key Factors should be interpreted as model influences, not necessarily causal explanations. Their purpose is to help sellers understand and investigate the prediction — not to encourage changing CRM fields simply to increase the score.

Important: If SAP-RPT is selected for Opportunity Scoring, only the Opportunity Score is displayed; Key Factors and the Insights section are not available.

 

 

Prerequisites and Readiness: Good Scoring Starts Before Training

Before asking “How do we activate scoring?”, the first question should be:

“Is our data ready to train a useful model?”

For Native scoring models, SAP provides dedicated Readiness Reports for Lead and Opportunity Scoring. These reports compare the minimum, recommended, and actual values for the relevant readiness criteria. A Red status indicates that requirements are not met, Orange that they are partially met, and Green that the recommended criteria have been reached.

 

Data Volume, Historical Coverage, and Model Choice

For a Native model, Machine Learning needs enough examples of both successful and unsuccessful outcomes to learn meaningful patterns.

For Lead Scoring, SAP specifies a minimum of 1,000 Leads converted into Opportunities and 1,000 Declined Leads. SAP's broader Lead Scoring Machine Learning guidance also recommends having at least six months to one year of historical data available for training.

For Deal Scoring, SAP specifies a minimum of 1,000 Won Opportunities and 1,000 Lost Opportunities for Native model training.

These Native data-volume requirements should not be treated as prerequisites for SAP-RPT. SAP-RPT is specifically recommended for customers whose dataset is insufficient to train a Native model.

This makes model choice part of the readiness discussion:

Enough representative historical data → consider Native
Insufficient data for Native training → evaluate SAP-RPT availability and fit

For Native models, the Readiness Report remains the primary validation tool. For Lead Scoring, the data-volume check specifically considers Leads that have been converted into Opportunities or moved to Declined status.

The key principle is:

Meeting the minimum data volume enables training; it does not guarantee a strong model.

A large CRM database does not automatically mean a large usable training dataset. What matters is having sufficient records with reliable outcomes, representative attributes, and meaningful historical behavior.

 

What Else Should Be Validated Before Training?

Before training a Native model, check:

  • Outcome quality: Are Converted/Declined and Won/Lost outcomes maintained correctly?
  • Completeness: Are relevant attributes populated consistently?
  • Historical relevance: Does older data still represent the way the company sells today?
  • Process consistency: Have sales phases, sources, priorities, territories, or qualification practices changed significantly?
  • Migration quality: If history came from another CRM, was its business meaning and lifecycle information preserved?
  • Custom data: Are customer-specific fields meaningful and populated often enough to contribute to the model?

Data quality is particularly important for Opportunity Scoring. SAP guidance highlights the importance of regularly recording opportunity outcomes — including Lost Opportunities — and notes that migrated opportunity data without the relevant change history can affect model training.

SAP Sales Cloud V2 also allows supported extension fields to participate in Lead and Deal Scoring. For Lead Scoring, SAP currently supports code-type extension fields and recommends ensuring sufficient data-volume presence before including them in the ML scenario. Removing extension fields already used by trained or active models can cause inference to fail.

For a Native model, the typical journey is:

Run Readiness → Create Model → Add relevant extensions if required → Train → Validate model performance → Activate → Complete initial scoring → Start adoption

Finally, data readiness and model performance are two separate gates:

Readiness asks: Can we train a meaningful model?
Model performance asks: Is the trained model good enough to activate?

For Native Lead and Opportunity Scoring models in a production tenant, SAP currently requires Prediction Confidence ≥ 95 and Predictive Power ≥ 60 before activation. SAP also recommends keeping only one model active for each scenario.

The following examples illustrate the Native scoring experience, where Key Factors and additional scoring insights are available.

 

 

Use Case 1: Lead Scoring – From Insight to Prioritization

Consider a seller reviewing an open lead that has not received attention for some time.

The lead has a Lead Score of 75 and is classified as “Very Likely to Convert.” At the same time, the record shows that there have been no activities for one month.

Data → Model → Score → Action → Outcome

  • Data: Historical Leads with reliable Converted and Declined outcomes provide the patterns used to train the Native Lead Scoring model.
  • Model: The model evaluates the current Lead against patterns learned from previous Lead outcomes.
  • Score: The Lead receives a score of 75 and is classified as Very Likely to Convert. The seller can also review the Dynamic and Static Key Factors influencing the prediction.
  • Seller action: Rather than allowing the Lead to remain unattended, the seller uses the score as a prioritization signal and investigates the current situation:
    • Why has there been no activity for one month?
    • Is the lead still relevant and correctly qualified?
    • Do the Key Factors support prioritizing renewed engagement?
    • Is any important information missing or outdated?
  • Potential outcome: A potentially valuable Lead receives attention earlier, helping the seller focus time on records that show stronger historical conversion characteristics.

The key principle is:

A high Lead Score should trigger prioritization and investigation — not automatic conversion.

 

Use Case 2: Deal Scoring – From Score to Coaching Conversation

Now imagine a sales manager preparing for a forecast review.

The opportunity has a Deal Score of 80, indicating relatively strong win characteristics. However, the same view also reveals signals that deserve attention: the opportunity is already 13 days past its close date, its phase progress is stalled, and some Key Factors are negatively influencing the prediction.

Data → Model → Score → Action → Outcome

  • Data: Historical Opportunities and their outcomes provide the patterns used to train the Native Deal Scoring model.
  • Model: The model evaluates the current Opportunity against patterns learned from previous sales outcomes.
  • Score: The deal receives a score of 80. The seller and manager can also review the Key Factors and Score Trend to better understand the prediction.
  • Manager and seller action: Instead of treating the high score as a signal that no further attention is required, they review the complete context:
    • Is the expected close date still realistic?
    • Why has the opportunity stopped progressing?
    • Are the latest customer interactions reflected in CRM?
    • Do the negative Key Factors indicate something that requires seller attention?
  • Potential outcome: The score becomes the starting point for a more informed pipeline conversation, combining the Machine Learning prediction with current deal context and seller knowledge.

The key principle is:

Do not interpret the score in isolation. Use the score, trend, influencing factors, and current context together to decide where attention is needed.

 

 

Known Considerations, Roadblocks & Troubleshooting

Even when the capability is technically available, several factors can reduce the value or reliability of scoring.

“We have a lot of data, so we are ready.”

Not necessarily. For Native models, volume alone is not enough. Inconsistent outcomes, missing fields, unbalanced data, or irrelevant history can still reduce model usefulness.

The sales process has changed significantly

A Native model trained on historical behavior may become less representative after major changes to products, territories, qualification methodology, or go-to-market strategy. Significant business changes should therefore trigger a review of model relevance and, where appropriate, retraining.

Historical data was migrated

A successful technical migration does not automatically mean the dataset is suitable for Machine Learning. Validate status mappings, historical meaning, field usage, and relevant lifecycle information before relying on the migrated history for Native model training.

Choosing the right model type

Native provides richer explainability through Key Factors and related insights but depends on sufficient representative historical data for training. SAP-RPT can support limited data scenarios but currently provides the Opportunity Score without Key Factors and is documented as restricted availability. Model choice should therefore consider both data readiness and the level of explainability required by the business.

The model is active, but no scores appear

Scores are not necessarily visible immediately after activation. SAP documents an initial scoring process that must be completed first. Lead and Opportunity score displays are then updated daily, triggered around midnight according to the data-center time zone.

Training does not progress as expected

For Deal Scoring, SAP KBA 3745937 – Opportunity Scoring Model is Stuck documents a case where insufficient training data prevents the model from progressing and recommends checking the Readiness Report.

For Lead Scoring, SAP KBA 3516688 addresses cases where the Readiness Report appears to show an unexpected data volume

Custom fields change after model creation

SAP warns against removing extension fields already used by trained or active scoring models. For Opportunity Scoring, deleting these fields can cause model training or inference to fail; similar inference risks are documented for Lead Scoring.

Users do not trust the score

This is an adoption challenge, not only a technical one. Position scoring as decision support and prioritization, not as an automated judgment of seller performance.

 

Adoption Best Practices: Activation is Only the Beginning

A successful scoring implementation needs more than technical activation. It requires a clear operating model around how the score is validated, used, monitored, and governed.

1. Start with the Business Decision

Define what should improve:

  • Lead prioritization
  • Pipeline inspection
  • Forecast conversations
  • Manager coaching

Without a clear action linked to the score, even a technically strong prediction can become just another CRM field.

2. Validate Before Broad Rollout

For Native models, review data readiness and model performance before activation, then validate representative business examples with sales experts.

Ask not only:

“Is the model technically valid?”

but also:

“Does its behavior make sense to people who understand our sales process?”

For SAP-RPT, validation should focus on whether the scoring behavior is useful for the business scenario and whether the reduced explainability — without Key Factors — is acceptable for users.

3. Pilot Before Scaling

Start with a representative group of sellers or managers. Use their feedback to validate score interpretation, seller actions, enablement needs, and how scoring should fit into existing sales processes before scaling to a broader user population.

4. Monitor Both Model and Business Performance

Technical model metrics matter for Native models, but they should always be complemented by business and adoption KPIs.

A model can perform technically well and still fail to create value if sellers do not understand or use the score.

Monitor whether scoring is actually influencing the intended decisions — for example, lead prioritization, pipeline reviews, or manager coaching.

5. Retrain And Revalidate Native Models

Historical patterns change.

For Native scoring models, SAP’s broader Machine Learning guidance recommends periodic retraining as the underlying data evolves, using approximately 6–10 months as a planning guideline.

This should not be treated as a fixed calendar rule. Significant changes may justify reviewing and retraining the model earlier, for example:

Data Migration → New Sales Processes → Major Product or Segment Changes → Changed Seller Behavior → Significant Shifts in Conversion or Win Patterns

After retraining, model performance and business relevance should be validated again before activating the new model.

SAP-RPT does not follow the same customer-specific retraining lifecycle, so this step applies specifically to Native models.

6. Establish Clear Governance

Define who owns:

Data Quality → Readiness → Model Validation → Activation → Adoption → Monitoring → Retraining

Governance should also define when the scoring approach itself should be reassessed — for example, if data volume improves enough to reconsider Native versus SAP-RPT.

Without clear ownership, scoring can gradually become disconnected from the business process it was designed to support.

 

Consultant Guidance: Should We Recommend Lead or Deal Scoring?

Before recommending Lead or Deal Scoring, consultants should assess two dimensions:

  • Technical readiness: Is the customer’s data, configuration, and model approach suitable for the scoring scenario?
  • Business readiness: Is there a clear decision, action, and ownership model around the score?

The following questions can be used as a practical customer readiness checklist:

Discovery Question

What “Ready” Looks Like

What business decision should scoring improve?

 

A clear seller or manager action is linked to the score.

Is sufficient historical data available?

For Native models, the Readiness Report supports model training and relevant positive and negative outcomes are represented.

 

Are outcomes reliable?

Converted/Declined and Won/Lost statuses reflect real business outcomes.

 

Is the data consistently maintained?

Relevant attributes are populated throughout the sales lifecycle.

 

Is historical data still representative?

The current sales process is sufficiently aligned with the process reflected in the historical data.

 

Was historical data migrated?

Data meaning, status mapping, and relevant lifecycle information have been validated.

 

Are custom fields required?

They are supported, meaningful, and sufficiently populated for the intended scenario.

 

Which model approach fits the customer?

Native when sufficient representative historical data exists; SAP-RPT can be evaluated for limited-data scenarios, considering availability and the absence of Key Factors.

 

Will sellers understand how to use the score?

Enablement covers score interpretation, insights, limitations, and expected seller actions.

 

Who owns scoring after go-live?

Ownership is defined for data quality, validation, adoption, monitoring, and Native-model retraining where applicable.

 

How will success be measured?

Business and adoption KPIs are agreed before rollout.

 

When Should Scoring Be Recommended?

Lead and Deal Scoring are strongest when the customer has:

  • a genuine lead-prioritization or pipeline-management problem;
  • a clear seller or manager action linked to the score;
  • reliable business data and outcomes;
  • a sales process that users understand and maintain consistently;
  • and ownership for adoption and ongoing governance.

Limited historical data does not necessarily rule out Deal Scoring in V2: SAP-RPT can be evaluated as an alternative where Native training data is insufficient, subject to availability and the customer’s explainability requirements.

However, if outcomes are unreliable, CRM data is poorly maintained, the sales process is unstable, or users cannot explain what they would do differently after seeing the score, improving data, process, and adoption readiness should come first.

A useful rule of thumb is:

If the organization cannot explain what a seller should do differently after seeing the score, the use case is not ready yet.

 

KPIs to Consider

Technical model performance matters for Native models, but business impact ultimately determines whether scoring is creating value.

For Lead Scoring, useful KPIs include conversion rate by score band, time to first meaningful contact, qualification time, and seller adoption.

For Deal Scoring, consider win rate by score band, pipeline aging, score evolution, and manager adoption.

The goal is not to maximize the ML score, but to improve the business decision enabled by it.

 

 

Final Thoughts

Lead and Deal Scoring can turn business data into a practical signal for sales prioritization, pipeline inspection, and coaching.

But the score itself is only the visible outcome. Its value depends on what sits behind it:

The Right Model Approach + Reliable Data + Meaningful Validation + Clear Seller Action + Continuous Governance

That combination is what turns Machine Learning from an interesting score on the screen into a useful part of the sales operating model.

So perhaps the most important question is not:

“How do we activate Lead and Deal Scoring?”

but rather:

“Do we have the right model, data, process, and actions in place to trust the score and act on it?”

When those foundations are in place, Lead and Deal Scoring can provide sellers and managers with a valuable second perspective — helping them focus attention, challenge assumptions, and make better-informed sales decisions.
